#6696. Upside-Down Cream Of Mushroom Tartlets

Upside-down tartlets went viral on social media, but they’re the party app we’re forever obsessed with. This hack uses store-bought puff pastry and transforms it into a beautiful, shareable snack filled with your sweet or savory filling of choice. Here, we’re leaning into cozy season by creating a cream of mushroom soup-inspired filling that pairs perfectly with the flaky pastry.

The mushrooms:You can find mushrooms used in two different ways here: both sliced and in a creamy, cheesy filling. The filling starts with a classic combination of minced mushrooms and shallots known as a duxelles (the very same mixture you can find at the base of a beef Wellington). To make this filling more mushroom soup-esque, we supplement it with Gùyere, heavy cream, and either sour cream or crème fraîche. The tangy dairy offsets some of the richness of the pastry while still containing enough fat to avoid curdling in the oven.

The pastry:When working with puff pastry, it’s important that you avoid prolonged exposure to heat. The dough is stacked with layers and layers of cold butter, which should melt and produce steam in the oven to create that signature flaky texture. Allowing that butter to melt while the dough sits on the counter will sacrifice that essential puff. If you notice your pastry start to warm up or stick to the counter, transfer it to a parchment-lined baking sheet, and let it cool down in the refrigerator for 10 to 15 minutes before you start working with it again.

Make ahead:The best part about this recipe is that you can make most of the components ahead of time. The mushroom filling can be made up to 3 days in advance, while the puff pastry squares can be cut and refrigerated up to a day before serving.

Did you make these tartlets? Rate and review them below!

#6695. The Best Greens Supplements to Boost Energy, Gut Health, and Skin

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The new generation of power powders does more than give you a daily serving of greens

With the wellness industry still booming, we’re inundated with products and devices that promise a shortcut to total health. Now, there’s a long list of gadgets, apps, topical creams, and ingestible supplements designed to clear your mind, calm your nervous system, boost energy, and improve sleep.

One supplement class that continues to reign in the mainstream is greens powders, more than just green juice in powder form. Below, the experts unpack everything you really need to know about the new generation of greens supplements.

These supercharged green food powders aren’t just specialty items at vitamin shops; you can now find them everywhere—from drugstores to Amazon. But according to Philippa May, co-founder of women-first greens powder brand Naere, the big players have one glaring problem: they’re created by men, for men.

“We created Nectar 01 as an antidote to the male-dominated market,” she says. “The highly successful green powders already in the category were built around male-focused language: performance, optimization, stronger. And supplements aimed at women often leaned into insecurities: de-bloat, anti-aging, fixing your skin, helping you ‘bounce back.’ We felt there was nothing truly speaking to women as they are, beyond problems to be solved, and instead as modern individuals navigating the natural flux of daily life, in need of support rather than correction.”

This is where the next generation of greens powders comes in. Sitting alongside Naere is the much-hyped LymaID²: the biohacking superbrand’s latest launch (and its most accessibly priced offering, too). Founder Lucy Goff enlists the most revered specialists in a field to power her revolutionary launches, so she created ID² in collaboration with Professor Paul Clayton, a clinical pharmacologist and senior scientific adviser to the U.K. government.

Similarly, Catherine Hurley has focused on organic powdered fruits and vegetables, rather than a long list of trendy ingredients that may appeal to the world’s biohacking bros. Her Newroad 30 powder contains a megadose of polyphenol-rich fruits and berries, alongside vegetables and pulses to support the gut microbiome. In short, it’s not a hack for superhuman fitness, but a real-food supplement to boost your existing diet.

Most of these powders contain greens—from common produce like spinach and kale to specialty greens like alfalfa grass and chlorophyll. These powders often also include fiber-rich foods, probiotic sources, and digestive enzymes to help further reduce bloating.

But what do the experts really think? Nutritionists largely agree that greens powders can support wellness, but only when paired with a healthy, varied diet. (If your core food groups are Pret sandwiches and cortisol, mainlining a glass of greens each morning won’t save you.)

“The starting point for me is always food,” says Jessica Shand, a naturopathic nutritionist and author of The Hormone Balance Handbook. “No powder will ever replace the benefits of eating a wide variety of vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, and seeds because whole foods provide so much more than individual vitamins and minerals alone. They contain fiber, polyphenols, phytonutrients, and thousands of interactions that we simply cannot fully replicate in a supplement,” she says.

That said, we also have to be realistic about how people live. “Busy schedules, frequent travel, limited access to fresh produce, or simply not consuming enough plant variety are all situations where a greens or plant powder may be helpful,” Shand adds. “However, I would only ever recommend a high-quality product, and, in my opinion, those are relatively few and far between.”

So, which greens powders are really worth investing in? Below, see the Bazaar breakdown of the supplements to stick to this year, all editor-tested.

Lyma is a brand known for moving the goalposts with its innovative (albeit investment-level) products, and ID²—the brand’s probiotic powdered supplement—is no different.

“The modern diet leaves most of us less than what we could be,” says Paul Clayton, a professor who worked with the brand on the launch. “Lyma ID² was built to put those elements back into place—the ones that the science of the longest-living people in human history told us matter most.”

Based on the philosophy that longevity begins with a healthy gut, ID² contains a diverse range of prebiotic fibers, since no single strain benefits every section of the gut, along with bioavailable omega-3s and a range of minerals and vitamins.

Personally, I saw a huge difference after drinking the formula religiously for six weeks, especially with bloating. By the one-month mark, my midafternoon brain fog had all but subsided. And thanks to the genuinely pleasant grapefruit taste, I’ve stuck with it for several months now.

Newroad 30 is a gut supplement containing 30 organic powdered fruits and vegetables. Rather than focusing on greens, which can be an acquired taste, founder Catherine Hurley has placed red fruits and berries at the center of her formula. “They provide a rich source of polyphenols and antioxidants that support gut health, skin health, and healthy aging,” she explains. “We still include vegetables and pulses, but their flavors sit behind the berry profile. The result is a product that delivers the benefits while tasting genuinely great, making it much easier to enjoy every day.” Indeed, if you’ve struggled to commit to an earthy greens powder before, this black-currant-tinged powder is the one to choose, delivering vitamins and minerals to support a healthy gut microbiome without the unpleasant taste.

Another benefit is how Newroad 30 is made. “We freeze-dry every ingredient. Most powders are spray-dried, and this method doesn’t preserve nutrients, fiber, and polyphenols as well as freeze-drying, which also preserves flavor,” says Hurley. Everything is organic here, too—an important consideration because, as Hurley explains, “the process of drying the ingredients concentrates any pesticides present.”

Lastly, what’s not in this plant-powered powder is as important as what is. “I would not want to take a powder with additives, such as sweeteners, flavorings, colors, emulsifiers, and binders,” Hurley adds, and Newroad 30 is free of them.

One of the longstanding powdered supplements on the market, Elle Macpherson’s The Super Elixir Daily Greens is particularly beneficial for those navigating hormonal shifts, such as perimenopause. Alongside prebiotics, four probiotic strains, adaptogenic botanicals, and powdered greens, it includes a cocktail of vitamins and minerals—from ginseng and glutamine to B vitamins—designed to boost energy and reduce brain fog. For the skin challenges that often come at this time (think: loss of laxity and dryness), it also includes biotin and zinc.

While this power cocktail won’t directly balance your hormones, it will provide a strong nutritional foundation to support the body through such a seismic shift. The taste is distinctly “green” (if you’re picky about flavor, expect a challenge), but the energy-boosting potential is real.

The original green powder, AG1, was made with athletes in mind but is for anyone who needs extra physical energy and mental clarity. Essentially, it’s a potent, well-rounded multivitamin that provides 100 percent of the RDA for key nutrients, including vitamins C and E, energy-providing B vitamins, two strains of gut-boosting probiotics, plant superfoods, and stress-reducing adaptogens.

Anecdotal praise for this one isn’t hard to find: Chances are, you already know one loyal devotee. However, the formula notably lacks iron, which, since women generally need more iron than men, points to the brand’s male-leaning marketing. Also, keep in mind the formula is a proprietary blend, so the brand doesn’t disclose the exact amount of each ingredient.

Built by women, for women, Naere brings ingredient transparency to the supplements space with its online Integrity Index™—a digital service that analyzes any supplement, from any brand, and delivers a detailed breakdown of its safety and efficacy based on your personal needs.

This uncompromising focus on quality over quantity naturally follows through into its debut launch, Nectar 01. This powdered supplement contains 30 ingredients—four of which are patented—significantly fewer than many competitors.

You can delve into every ingredient on the brand’s website, but the headliners are marine-derived hydrolyzed collagen peptides and sodium hyaluronate to support skin and joints; algae-derived astaxanthin for antioxidant protection; selenium for immune function; and a patented black pepper extract to improve the bioavailability of the other ingredients.

“Ultimately, the best supplements aren’t about including everything, but about choosing well-dosed, bioavailable ingredients that genuinely deliver,” says co-founder Philippa May. “And most importantly, consistency always wins. One supplement you take daily will always beat the supplement stack you forget.”

This is another one I found easy to stick to. The slightly sweet, green taste is peculiar but not unpleasant, and after finishing my first package, I saw real improvements in my bloating and digestion, plus steadier energy levels.

#6692. Taylor Swift’s Surprise Grammys Nomination Appearance Came With Easter Eggs

Taylor Swift made Grammys history this morning, joining Kendrick Lamar as the only other artist to have five consecutive albums nominated for Album of the Year. But the singer also made a surprise appearance during the nomination announcement broadcast. In a video, she introduced the two biggest categories, Album of the Year and Song of the Year. She kept her look simple, wearing a black sweater. But fans homed in on her accessories, which included a large horseshoe necklace. Her second necklace continued the cowgirl theme with its horse charm.

Swift has worn the horseshoe necklace multiple times before, including at the Toy Story 5 premiere in June. The horseshoe seems to be an Easter egg for her Toy Story 5 song, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” which is about the movie’s cowgirl character Jessie. The track was nominated for Song of the Year and Best Song Written for Visual Media this morning.

The second necklace, featuring a horse’s head in a curved, horseshoe-shaped frame, is another nod to Jessie, who rides toy horse Bullseye in the movie.

Initially, some fans thought the second necklace had a snake charm. The singer has drawn attention for wearing snake jewelry before. In March 2025, fans noticed one during her virtual appearance at the iHeartRadio Music Awards. Snakes have long been associated with Swift’s Reputation era, and Swifties have been waiting for years for her to release the rerecorded Taylor’s Version of that album.

When Swift bought back her first six albums’ masters in May 2025, she gave fans an update on that project in a public letter. “I know, I know. What about Rep TV?” she wrote. “Full transparency: I haven’t even rerecorded a quarter of it. The Reputation album was so specific to that time in my life, and I kept hitting a stopping point when I tried to remake it. All that defiance, that longing to be understood while feeling purposely misunderstood, that desperate hope, that shame-born snarl and mischief. To be perfectly honest, it’s the one album in those first six that I thought couldn’t be improved upon by redoing it. Not the music, or photos, or videos. So I kept putting it off. There will be a time (if you’re into the idea) for the unreleased Vault tracks from that album to hatch.”

In her video today, Swift congratulated her fellow artists and playfully reflected on her own history with the two categories she presented. She said, “Good morning, America, it’s Taylor. I’m very honored that the Grammys have asked me to be here to help reveal the last two categories for the Grammy nominations. And I first wanted to start off by saying congratulations to anyone who’s nominated for a Grammy this year in any category because what this means is that your peers—your fellow musicians, producers, engineers, artists, writers—they love what you made. And that’s the coolest feeling in the world. I hope you have a really wonderful day. The last two categories to be announced, one of them I’ve had a lot of luck in [Album of the Year, which she has won four times], and the other one I’m zero for eight. Here are the nominees for Album and Song of the Year.”

#6691. Wendy's Is Making Major Changes To Its Menu—Including A Creamier Frosty

Wendy's is giving its classics an upgrade.

Wendy's is betting that better bacon and a creamier Frosty could help its sales slump. After reporting another decline in U.S. sales, the fast food chain is testing changes to several of its best-known menu items. This refresh will appear on the menu at some point in 2027, according to Fox News.

The most interesting update might be the Frosty, which Wendy's is working to make richer and creamier. The chain hasn't revealed the exact recipe changes, but given how recognizable the dessert has become, I'm curious how much the new version will differ. Whether or not it wins over fans who already know and love the original consistency is also up in the air.

Then there's the bacon. Wendy's is testing thicker, crispier bacon that could give sandwiches like the Baconator a more substantial bite. Personally, I think this is a pretty smart move. There's nothing more disappointing than ordering a bacon cheeseburger and barely noticing the bacon.

The chain is also experimenting with whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches and upgraded salads, all part of an effort to improve the quality of its existing menu rather than relying entirely on new products.

These changes aren’t coming out of nowhere. Wendy's reported a 5.7% decline in U.S. same-restaurant sales during the third quarter of 2026, marking another difficult period for the chain. In response, CEO Bob Wright is introducing a multi-year turnaround strategy called “Dave's Way,” named after Wendy's founder Dave Thomas.

The strategy focuses on improving the menu, marketing, restaurant operations, and digital ordering experience while giving customers better value for their money. But depending on your nearest location, it might come at a cost: breakfast.

Wendy's is allowing franchise operators to decide whether offering breakfast makes financial sense for their individual restaurants. That means some locations could stop serving breakfast altogether, although the company isn't eliminating the morning menu nationwide.

Wendy's also plans to simplify its offerings by removing lower-selling items that make restaurant kitchens more complicated to operate. However, the chain hasn't provided a complete list of products that could disappear.

The chain is still testing upgraded ingredients, so we won’t know the extent of the menu refresh or when it’ll roll out until some point in 2027. But if you’re anything like me, you’ll be waiting with bated breath to see how Wendy’s changes one of the most iconic fast food desserts.

#6690. Everything You Need to Know About Korean Scalp Scalers

If you’ve ever been to a Korean head spa, you know it’s less a hair wash than a full reset. Before reaching for the shampoo, a technician typically examines your scalp with a magnifying camera, then applies a treatment to loosen the oil, dead skin, and product residue a regular wash leaves behind. It’s the step that makes your hair feel impossibly light afterward, and it’s called scaling.

You don’t need a spa appointment to get the same effect, though. Scalp scalers bring that deep clean home, whether that’s an acid-based treatment you leave on before shampooing or a salt scrub that lathers up in the shower. They’re especially useful if you lean on dry shampoo, work out often, or have fine hair that goes flat a day after washing.

Below, experts explain what a scalp scaler does, who should use one, how to avoid overdoing it, and which formulas are worth trying.

The name actually comes from the dentist’s office. “In Korean, ‘scaling’ is the same word we use for dental cleaning,” says Ellie Byun, a doctor of Korean medicine and licensed acupuncturist. “Plaque builds up on your teeth even when you brush, and in the same way, oil and dead skin build up on your scalp even when you shampoo.” For many Korean women, it’s a familiar routine. “I’ve been using scalp scalers since high school,” says Kristin Lim, founder of Base-K.

Some scalers work differently from regular shampoos because they require additional time on the scalp. “A clarifying shampoo only cleanses during the short time it’s on your scalp,” Dr. Byun says. “A scaler stays on for several minutes and chemically dissolves dead skin and oil with acids and enzymes—the same principle as an exfoliating toner for your face.”

That’s true of some chemical scalers, but others, including several below, use salt granules instead of acids, or a combination of chemical and physical exfoliants. “A scalp scaler focuses on loosening dead skin and buildup, using acids, physical exfoliants, or a combination of both,” Lim says.

If you go the gritty route, keep it gentle. “A scrub physically buffs the surface with grains, and if you use it too often, it can make the scalp barrier sensitive,” Dr. Byun says. “It’s especially good for oily scalps, flaking caused by buildup, fine hair that goes flat quickly, people who use a lot of dry shampoo and styling products, and anyone who sweats a lot.”

Flaking is where it gets tricky, though. “It can also help loosen surface flakes, but persistent flaking and itching deserve a closer look,” Lim says. “Dandruff and other scalp conditions may need targeted treatment rather than more exfoliation.”

The first thing most people notice is how light their hair feels afterward. “Removing that residue can leave the scalp feeling cleaner and the hair feeling lighter,” Lim says. With regular use, it can reduce oil and flaking. Some research suggests that exfoliating ingredients can help address scalp flaking and discomfort. In one small study, a four-week regimen containing salicylic acid and other scalp-care ingredients improved dandruff, itching, redness, and oiliness in people with seborrheic dermatitis. However, the results don’t necessarily apply to every scalp scaler. Improving scalp health may also benefit hair quality over time. “Studies show that when scalp health declines, hair quality declines too, and when the scalp recovers, hair quality recovers with it,” Dr. Byun says.

The biggest risk is doing too much. “Over-exfoliating weakens the scalp barrier and can cause irritation, dryness, and even a rebound increase in oil,” Dr. Byun says. It’s not the right fit for every scalp, either. “Individuals with sensitive or irritated scalps should approach exfoliating treatments cautiously,” says Joe Cho, team lead of media relations at Medicube. Even a product labeled gentle may cause problems. “Even a gentle formula may not suit a scalp that’s actively inflamed,” Lim says. If something feels off, don’t push through it. “If you notice sudden heavy shedding, pain, or lesions, see a professional,” Dr. Byun says.

“Some scalers go onto a dry or damp scalp before shampooing, while others are used on wet hair as part of the wash,” Lim says. Either way, the product needs to reach your scalp, not just your hair. “Part your hair in sections about an inch apart and apply it directly to the scalp along each part,” Dr. Byun says. “Then massage with your fingertips, never your nails, for two to three minutes, pressing slowly on the crown and the base of the skull.” Then rinse it out on time. “Leaving it on longer or scrubbing harder won’t improve the result,” Lim says. Because formulas vary, follow the timing and application instructions on your particular product.

Less is more when it comes to frequency too. “I recommend once a week for oily scalps and once every two weeks for normal or dry scalps,” Dr. Byun says. Your scalp will tell you when you’ve gone too far. “Signs you’re overdoing it include tightness, stinging, redness, or tenderness, more flaking instead of less, new itching, or a scalp that feels oilier than before.” Lim also recommends sticking to one exfoliant at a time and avoiding combining several scalp exfoliants in the same wash.

Afterward, think of your scalp the way you’d think about your face after an exfoliating toner. “Korean care follows a simple idea—clear first, then nourish,” Dr. Byun says. “Use a mild, low-pH shampoo, then a lightweight scalp serum with niacinamide, panthenol, or centella, and apply conditioner only from the midlengths to the ends.”

Not directly. “While scalp health plays an important role in overall hair care, there’s currently limited clinical evidence that scalp exfoliation alone can directly stimulate hair growth or prevent shedding,” Cho says. Dr. Byun sees it as groundwork. “A scaler doesn’t grow hair on its own, but it does have a real, research-backed role,” she says. “So I see scaling as the first step in creating an environment where healthy hair can grow.” Lim is just as clear: “Promising that a scaler alone will regrow hair or stop shedding would be overpromising.”

Many scalp scalers can be used on color-treated hair, but it’s important to check the product’s instructions, since some exfoliating ingredients and cleansing formulas may affect color longevity. “It’s generally fine on color-treated hair as long as you apply it to the scalp, not the hair itself,” Dr. Byun says.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—for professional insight into the industry’s standout products these specialists would use themselves or recommend to their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For Korean scalp scalers, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, exfoliant type, texture, packaging, finish, and the hair-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6688. McDonald's Fans Are Celebrating The Return Of A Holiday Favorite They've Waited All Year For

McDonald's may be best known for its Big Mac burgers and mouthwatering fries, but that doesn't mean customers only frequent the chain for its classic menu items. In fact, fans are just as excited about some of the restaurant's seasonal offerings. Take its Holiday Pie, for instance. McDonald's introduced the limited-time dessert back in 1999, and it has consistently attracted customers for decades.

Like Mariah Carey thawing out for Christmas, McDonald’s Holiday Pie is finally back. The handheld dessert features creamy custard in a buttery crust, glazed with sugar, and topped with rainbow sprinkles.

The pie typically returns around November, although it's only available at select McDonald's restaurants. According to Allrecipes, fans have already spotted it in several cities this year, including New York, Philadelphia, and Boston, so if you're hoping to get your hands on one, your best bet is to check to see whether your local restaurant has it.

And the enthusiasm for this dessert is no joke. "Bruh they genuinely sold out in my area already," one fan commented on social media.

"Bro, this pie is delicious," another person wrote, while someone else had much bigger plans, sharing they’ll "probably eat 10 over the next two months!"

"Was hoping this was gonna return. Love the holiday pie," a different person commented. And someone else was already stocking up, writing, "I've ordered 2 yesterday and one was exactly sweet as I expected. Will try to get more before season time is done."

Of course, even a beloved holiday treat isn't immune to complaints about the price. During last year's release, one person wrote in a Reddit thread, "The holiday pie is my favorite, but pies are $2.89 here now and it's hard to justify spending $3 after tax on one." Another said their location had raised the price to $3.89 for a single pie.

Prices still vary by restaurant. For this year's return, one reviewer reported a price of $2.39 for one pie or $3.89 for two at their local Los Angeles McDonald's.

I guess you'll have to decide whether it's worth another taste of the holiday magic.

#6687. Ayo Edebiri Got the Forehead Curl Memo

Ayo Edebiri is one of the best-dressed people in Hollywood. In 2024, GQ named her a rising star in menswear. At our 2026 Men of the Year party, she made an even stronger case for herself as a style icon for the ages. Walking the red carpet at the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, the Emmy-winning actor continued her winning streak of power suiting in a navy chalk-stripe ensemble, a bright emerald-turquoise dress shirt, and a burgundy geometric tie. Her bob was styled in a side part, with a pronounced curl sweeping across her forehead. It’s a look that’s become a staple among Hollywood’s best-dressed men this year, a callback to Superman’s signature swoop, minus the Spandex tights and cape.

In the 1920s, the playful wisp of hair was known as the kiss curl: a deliberately placed lock of hair that sat on the forehead, even amid an otherwise carefully sculpted ’do. (As Seth Rogen helpfully pointed out on Instagram after we noted the kiss curl’s 2026 resurgence: “It’s called a Forelock.”) Its prominence in men’s grooming can be traced back in part to the French-American entertainer Josephine Baker, whose iconic curl ushered in an era—and now a century—of rogue forehead curls.

The kiss curl was so emblematic of the era that it made a triumphant return at the 2025 Met Gala, themed “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” A host of women paired the look with impeccable tailoring, including Simone Biles, Taraji P. Henson, Teyana Taylor, and, yes, Ayo Edebiri.

The modern appeal of the forehead curl is easy to understand. As hairstyles have grown longer, looser, and less structured, the curl lends an air of studied nonchalance—as if you didn’t spend too much time getting your hair just right. It’s sexy in a just-got-out-of-bed kind of way, especially when everything else—from the rest of the hair to the outfit—remains crisp, clean, and pristine.

As Edebiri once told Vogue of dressing for the red carpet: “One of the fun parts of getting to do this sort of thing is that you get to transform and be these different permutations of yourself.” At GQ’s Men of the Year party, she once again understood the assignment.

#6685. The Wide-Leg Jeans That Every French Girl (And Kate Moss) Owns

Last month, while taking in the spring/summer 2027 shows at Paris Fashion Week, I was eager to write about the street style trends bubbling up around the showgoers in town. Which proved harder than anticipated. For one thing, the flashiest dressers had been given full looks by the brands whose shows they were being paid to attend, and reporting on those felt like a somewhat dishonest exercise in journalism. For another, the consensus seems to be that we are living in a post-trend world, and fashion people in particular have little interest in dressing like anyone else. And so I turned my attention to real-life Parisians, among whom one item seemed to proliferate: jeans.

No, this isn’t going to be a trend report on something as perennially popular as denim, but on a particular high-waisted, flared style that I spotted so frequently, I was forced to dredge up what little French remains from my GCSEs to ask a woman where hers were from as I caught her climbing onto a Lime bike outside Le Saint-Gervais bar. “Excuse-moi, madame, votre pantalons… le brand?” She paused for a moment, swung her leg over the saddle, and unleashed a torrent of French from which I managed to decipher just two words: “Anna” and “Gérard Darel”, the latter needing no explanation.

Founded in Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the 1970s, the brand has long been a shorthand for what the rest of the world considers the tenets of French-girl style: discreet, easy-to-wear classics with a cultivated air. (So cultivated, in fact, that the brand acquired the original handwritten Proust Questionnaire in 2003, and recently collaborated with the philosopher Alain de Botton on a card-game version.) Which is all very Left Bank, of course, but perhaps the clearest evidence of its credentials is just how commonplace Gérard Darel is in everyday Parisian life. You can scarcely move for its iconic 24H bag—a soft, logo-free shoulder bag that Vogue once named among the bags of the century, alongside the Hermès Birkin – during the school rush on the Métro, where it is generally to be found stuffed with binders and tangled wired headphones.

But back to the jeans–an American invention, admittedly, but then again, this is the land of French fries. What made my startled Parisienne’s look so good? Much of it comes down to the cut–something Kate Moss, a woman who found fame in nothing more than a pair of jeans, understands, having been photographed in the brand’s Anna jeans as early as 2019. Designed by former creative director Valérie Gerbi and named after her daughter Anna – granddaughter of the brand’s founders, Danièle and Gérard Darel–the design braces at just the right point on the hips, fits snugly through the thighs and flares outwards just below the knee, skimming the top of a pair of shoes to create the illusion of longer legs. The double belt loops, meanwhile, criss-cross along the waistband to give the impression of a cinched waist, while the back pockets perform a similarly flattering service for the bum.

And yet the technicalities of a good fit can only explain so much. Perhaps the true appeal was in the way she wore them–with white ballet flats that I’m convinced were from Repetto’s men’s section (the Luciens) and a navy three-quarter-zip jumper with the sleeves pushed up–or the ease with which disappeared into the Marais, hair whipping in the wind.

#6683. Andrew Garfield’s Hair Is the Mane Attraction

Andrew Garfield’s hair is very long—and oh so glorious. When the 43-year-old actor sat down with GQ for his 2026 Men of the Year interview, he told us he’d grown his current shoulder-length mane for his role as Roy Horn (of Siegfried & Roy tiger-wrangling fame) in the upcoming series Wild Things. Production ultimately put him in a wig, but Garfield kept the length regardless. And thank goodness he did. The actor brought his enviable mane to the red carpet at our annual Men of the Year party at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles on Thursday night, where it held its own among Hollywood’s finest.

The Artificial star arrived in an Edward Sexton suit, accessorized with a Breguet watch. But, as has been the case lately, his hair was the real headliner. The neck-grazing length was in fine form, with a few stray strands tucked neatly behind his ears. And then there was the forehead curl: a particularly on-trend flourish that’s found its place atop some of this year’s best-dressed stars (including Ayo Edebiri).

We first caught a glimpse of Garfield’s longer locks at Wimbledon this summer in London. At the time, his longtime hairstylist, Lucy Halperin, let us in on the secret to the look: a little sea salt spray, styling cream, and a diffuser to bring out his natural curls and waves. The combination enhances the hair’s volume while keeping frizz at bay.

That said, Halperin also credits his good hair to a bit of genetic luck. “Sometimes we just give it a good little wet down, and it kind of just works with him,” she told us at the time.

Whatever transformations Garfield has in store for his next on-screen role, we hope this particular look sticks around. Because if Thursday night was any indication, he’s not quite ready to part with it—and frankly, neither are we.

#6682. Robert Pattinson Is the James Bond Millennials Deserve

The 40-year-old actor has been chosen to become the seventh James Bond in film, following in the footsteps of Daniel Craig

The news is finally out: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond. After weeks of speculation and an almost algorithmic audition process that played out on our social feeds, Pattinson has triumphed over a list of peers that reportedly included Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

For the last few weeks, I’ve watched the rolling news coverage of the casting process with trepidation, because the concept of a machismo-fueled, womanizing killing machine feels tired and outdated in 2026. But that’s exactly why the choice of Pattinson made me breathe a sigh of relief. Since breaking out in the 2000s,Pattinson’s career has been defined by his willingness to subvert traditional masculine archetypes, crafting them instead into slightly twisted leading-man roles. From his starring role in 2022’s The Batman to the 2026 rom-com The Drama and most recently the disturbing Oscar-tipped biopic Primetime, he has often looked for ways to subvert our expectations of the classic leading man. If there’s one actor who just might be able to make 007 feel aspirational and relevant again, it’s him.

From the beginning, Pattinson, who first emerged as a teen icon in the Twilight movies, has represented a counter-argument to traditional, protein-based masculinity. “Team Edward” and “Team Jacob,” the franchise’s central romantic rivalry (and marketing ploy), offered two very different visions of male desirability. Jacob, played by Taylor Lautner, was part man, part wolf, and was muscular, physically imposing, and (thankfully) almost always shirtless, which today draws more of a visual parallel with the sort of hypermasculinity that has flourished in online gym-bro culture and the so-called “manosphere.” And then there was Edward, Pattinson’s pale, brooding vampire who was more sensitive and emotionally tortured. With the selection of a new Bond, it feels like we’re once again seeing this masculine power struggle play out—and again, it’s Pattinson who has come out on top.

In the packed field of chiseled, handsome, talented actors who were vying for this role, whoever snagged it was always going to have his work cut out. As an archetype, 007 is a relic of generations gone by. The flashy gadgets, the signature martini, the expensive cars, and the ability to charm almost any woman belong to a very particular, nostalgic vision of masculinity. Through a more contemporary lens, Bond is the ultimate masculine drag act: an exaggerated, prop-heavy performance that is just as likely to be viewed as regressive and cliché.

We see the same trend in Bond’s dwindling romantic appeal. In our grandparents’ generation, when the character was at peak aspiration, a man arriving in a nice suit, carrying flowers, and driving a flashy car was considered a catch. But today, the dynamics have changed. I recently read The Project, the debut novel by British Vogue columnist Annie Lord, where she makes the observation that many of the most common dating “icks” now stem from men trying too hard: putting themselves out there too much, making an overt display of their interest, or seeming too confident. Lord notes that we’ve become accustomed to viewing these qualities as undesirable or embarrassing, which draws clear parallels with Bond, whose entire appeal has rested on this sort of performance. The spy’s extravagance and his carefully cultivated image were once what made him attractive, but can you imagine going on a date with a guy who seriously asks for his martini to be “shaken, not stirred”? You’d probably tell your group chat about it and endlessly mock him.

Looking more widely, there is also the question of whether the Bond franchise’s particular type of escapism can still work in the fraught world we’re currently living in. The franchise once offered a fantastical vision of evil, with megalomaniacs plotting world domination in ways that felt almost comically removed from reality. (Remember Bond’s “invisible” car in 2002’s Die Another Day?) But now, the real world feels uncomfortably close to that fantasy. Billionaires wield the kind of influence once reserved for nation-states, and the increasingly overt relationship between money and power makes it harder to distinguish the Bond villain caricature from what we’re encountering in day-to-day life.

Part of the reason Pattinson landed this role, I suspect, is that he already has experience in navigating nostalgic expectations and present-day anxieties. In The Batman, for example, he proved his ability to bring new dimensions to an old-school character with his tortured take on Bruce Wayne. And as a versatile actor who can move between action blockbusters, rom-coms, and critically acclaimed projects like Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, he has the star power and the credibility to give Bond a millennial makeover.

It’s worth saying that during Daniel Craig’s tenure as Bond, considerable effort was made to turn Bond into a deeper, more considered character. Craig’s films explored Bond’s childhood trauma and alcohol dependence, and they also introduced female characters who were more than just a sidekick or a throwaway romantic interest. But in the five years since Craig departed, a loud and unrepentant misogyny has taken hold in corners of the internet. And from the Epstein files to the Cornell University rape allegations and, most recently, the conviction of Russell Brand, so many stories come back to the central issue of toxic masculinity.

The wider conversation about male behavior has made casting the next Bond feel strangely high-stakes, which is probably why every screen test seemed to be leaked and endlessly dissected online. And it’s also why I’m relieved that they’ve picked an actor who might be able to make Bond a little more strange. Pattinson presents the opportunity to take Bond in a different direction—one that finally frees the character from the fantasies of the past.

#6680. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Republic Brands Group has acquired Rebecca Minkoff, which was founded by Minkoff and her brother Uri in 2005. The acquisition comes as the brand enters a new phase of growth following a successful transition to an asset-light licensing model, according to the company. Republic Brands plans to expand the brand’s international footprint and retail partnerships, with the view of doubling the business in 2027. Minkoff, who is chief creative officer, will remain closely involved in the brand’s creative direction under its new ownership.

Investor(s): Republic Brands Group (portfolio includes: Jason Wu, Christian Siriano, Joie)

Investor comments: “Rebecca Minkoff represents exactly the type of brand we believe has tremendous untapped potential,” Sami Souid, founder and CEO of Republic Brands Group, said in a statement. “It has strong consumer recognition, an authentic design identity and significant opportunities for global expansion. Our strategy is to unlock that potential through best-in-class operating partners, disciplined brand management and a focused approach to building a global lifestyle business.”

Company description: Founded in 2023, Counsel Health is an AI-powered primary care platform that combines medical AI with a network of physicians to deliver personalized medical guidance and treatment. The company has agreed to be acquired by Finnish smart ring maker Oura for $625 million, as Oura looks to move beyond biometric tracking toward more holistic, tailored health insights and actionable medical care. The acquisition will integrate Counsel’s AI and on-demand physicians with Oura’s continuous health data collection, enabling users to access medical advice, prescriptions, lab result interpretations, and chronic care support through the Oura app.

Funding and round: Acquisition, $625 million.

Investor comments: “Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale. “Together, we can create a new model of care that extends the current healthcare paradigm by delivering an experience that’s more immediate, personalized, and proactive.”

Company description: Founded in 1889, Lee has made its marks as one of the biggest heritage names in denim. The American brand generates an average of $1.5 billion in annual sales across 73 countries, of which almost 40% comes from outside the US and Canada. New York-based Authentic Brands Group has successfully acquired Lee from Kontoor Brands in an effort to expand Lee into adjacent categories, including activewear and workwear, as well as lifestyle offerings.

Investor(s): Authentic Brands Group (portfolio includes: Guess, Juicy Couture, Reebok).

Investor comments: “We are thrilled to welcome Lee to the Authentic family,” said Jamie Salter, founder and executive chair of Authentic Brands Group. “Lee has the heritage, recognition and consumer loyalty we look for in a brand. By connecting Lee to Authentic’s global platform and the right partners in key markets, we see a significant opportunity to expand its reach through content, experiences and new product categories.”

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Solomei AI, the company behind the Callimacus platform, has announced that it has entered into an agreement for an investment from Salesforce. The investment will “support Callimacus’s efforts to expand its engineering and AI research capabilities, accelerate product development, and scale commercial operations across Europe and North America.” In January 2026, Callimacus, whose chairman is Brunello Cucinelli, was used to build the new e-commerce experience for the designer’s eponymous luxury brand.

Investor comments: “Brunello has always believed that technology should elevate humanity, and that conviction is at the heart of Callimacus,” said Marc Benioff, chair and CEO of Salesforce. “The team has developed an innovative platform that reimagines AI-powered experiences — bringing together conversational AI, enterprise context, and real-time personalization to create entirely new ways for businesses to engage with their customers.”

“Three years ago, Marc Benioff and I began an endeavor with mathematicians, philosophers, humanists, and technologists, from which Callimacus was born. Our idea was to create a simple, intuitive product capable of speaking the language of human beings; a sort of new web, without pages, categories, or predetermined paths, able to accompany the intent of each individual navigator. I look with great confidence and hope for the path that Callimacus will pursue with Salesforce’s investment,” Brunello Cucinelli, chairman of Solomei AI, added.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Merit is a US-based beauty brand designed as an antidote to using multiple, trend-led products — collapsing everyday cosmetics into a curated, minimal line-up. The investment is led by Vasiliki Petrou, managing partner at Semcap Beauty & Wellness, who also founded the Unilever Prestige division in 2014, spanning Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice, Hourglass, K18, and more.

Investor comments: “Merit is one of the most thoughtfully built brands in beauty, a true icon in the market. I love the timeless brand aesthetic, the simplified and edited approach to beauty, and the focus on the millennial and Gen X consumer, which is a significant white space in our industry. I am thrilled to support the continued global scaling of the brand,” Petrou said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28% (up from 26.06%), which demands an official takeover bid in line with German legislation. The move follows Frasers’s €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss believed was “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Frasers, now Hugo Boss’s largest shareholder, said its offer still stands through July 27.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Syntetica is a French startup that transforms textile waste into recycled nylon through a proprietary chemical method that allows the processing of fabrics containing multiple materials. The funding will help Syntetica build its first commercial facility in France, which will be able to transform hundreds of tons of post-consumer textile waste annually. While Syntetica already works with labels such as Victoria’s Secret and Etam, it also plans to scale its recycling efforts and partner with more fashion brands.

Funding and round: $30 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Ecotechnologies 2 (portfolio includes: Standing Ovation, Mantle8), Lululemon (portfolio includes: Epoch Biodesign, Samsara Eco, Zymochem), MAS Holdings (portfolio includes: Victoria’s Secret, Calvin Klein, Gap), Swen Capital Partners, EQT Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal, Fleek is a wholesale vintage fashion marketplace. Fleek connects retailers and resellers with verified, secondhand clothing wholesalers worldwide, enabling them to source vintage inventory in bulk through a digital marketplace with integrated logistics and quality assurance.

Funding and round: $25 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Burda Principal Investments (portfolio includes: Vinted), Ebay Ventures, FJ Labs, H14, Andreessen Horowitz, HV Capital, Y Combinator, and more.

Company description: Whering is a digital wardrobe and styling app founded in 2020 by Bianca Rangecroft. The app enables users to catalogue the clothes they already own, create outfits, track wardrobe usage, and receive styling recommendations, with the aim of encouraging more intentional fashion consumption and reducing unnecessary purchases.

Investor(s): Ebay Ventures, Google AI Futures Fund.

Company description: Hair technology company Halo has developed its first product, HaloBraid. Launching in salons this fall, the device will be the first automated hair braiding tool that works alongside stylists to halve braiding time from as long as 10 hours per appointment. Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s VC firm Seven Seven Six is leading the investment into a business that was launched off the back of Yinka Ogunbiyi’s winning Harvard Innovation Labs pitch last year.

Investor(s): Seven Seven Six (portfolio includes: Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Flock Safety), Bling Capital (portfolio includes: Palantir, Gusto, Everlane), AlleyCorp (portfolio includes: ShopMy, Gilt Groupe, Business Insider).

Investor comments: “As an investor, I look for founders that see something broken that everyone else has accepted as fixed. Braiding is a perfect example: it is a process that has not materially changed in thousands of years, despite being one of the most popular hairstyles for millions of Americans and a significant part of the $270 billion salon services industry,” said Ohanian. “Yinka has introduced a novel technology to a traditionally manual and highly specialized professional service.”

Company description: L’Oréal Group has taken a stake in Indian personal care company Innovist. (Vogue Business reported on speculations back in March.) The company has a successful portfolio that includes Indian haircare brand Bare Anatomy, skincare brands Chemist at Play and Sunscoop, and bodycare brand Vinci Botanicals. The company was founded in 2018 by Rohit Chawla, Sifat Khurana, and Vimal Bhola with a focus on science-first formulations, transparent ingredients, and in-house research and development.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L’Oréal Group (portfolio includes: Cerave, La Roche-Posay, Vichy, Armani Beauty, SkinCeuticals).

Investor comments: “Our investment in this innovative Indian startup is a clear testament to our unwavering commitment to expanding L’Oréal’s footprint in India,” CEO Nicolas Hieronimus said. “By bringing together the very best of L’Oréal’s global expertise with Innovist’s high-performing, science-led products and deep-rooted understanding of the Indian consumer, I believe we are poised to shape the future of beauty in this dynamic market.”

Company description: Remedy is a dermatologist-developed skincare brand founded by Dr. Muneeb Shah in March 2024. The brand’s products target skin concerns such as dark spots, dryness, fine lines, dullness, keratosis pilaris, and sensitive skin. Remedy is stocked on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Target, the latter of which it partnered with in December 2025. The Series A investment will support the skincare brand with its next phase of growth, including advancing clinical research, expanding its product categories, and improving inventory. Remedy also plans to strengthen its formulation, testing, and consumer education.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L Catterton (portfolio includes: Merit Beauty, Tula, Kopari, Elemis, Nutrafol, Intercos, Ex Nihilo).

Investor comments: “We seek to partner with exceptional founders building brands that will redefine categories, and we believe Remedy is uniquely modernizing dermatological skincare,” L Catterton partner Tehmina Haider said. “As both a clinician and a consumer educator, Dr. Shah has built a portfolio of simple, effective, and accessibly priced products that leverage advanced ingredient technologies to address real patient needs — and that is what will define the next generation of dermocosmetics. The brand’s rapid growth reflects deep consumer demand for affordable, clinically-grounded skincare, and we are thrilled to partner with the Remedy team on its next chapter.”

Company description: Bacchus is a London-based PR agency founded in 1998 by Anouschka Menzies and Charlotte Lurot, who currently lead the business alongside co-CEO Daize Washbourn. The agency specializes in luxury hospitality and culture, as well as in the prestige VIC and high-net-worth communities. With around 100 employees across seven offices (London, New York, Miami, LA, Dubai, Riyadh, and Doha), Bacchus generates annual sales of approximately $17 million. Its client portfolio includes Red Sea Global Residences, Six Senses, Auberge Resorts, the Victoria & Albert Museum, and Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer.

Funding and round: Acquisition, majority stake.

Investor(s): Mazarine Group (portfolio includes: La Mode en Images, the show producer of Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Gucci).

Investor comments: “There were several objectives [with this investment],” Mazarine founder Paul-Emmanuel Reiffers tells Vogue Business. “First, we needed to add a public relations and influence branch to our group. Second, it had to be large enough for us to develop and accelerate it. With Bacchus, we’re starting from a platform that’s already large enough to consolidate operations, grow further, and open an office in Paris in the short to medium-term. Third, the acquisition gives us seven offices at once, providing an established global network and strengthening our geographic footprint. We already had a presence in Dubai, but now we’re able to establish ourselves in Riyadh, which is important because the Middle East is about to rebound strongly. We’re also strengthening our position in the US by expanding our network from New York to LA and Miami, allowing us to serve clients more effectively.”

He continues: “Finally, the acquisition aligns with what we see as the luxury sectors of tomorrow: hospitality, real estate, and longevity. As luxury brands increasingly move into these areas, we are positioning ourselves to support their expansion. It also creates valuable synergies, allowing us to integrate Bacchus’s expertise and network of personalities, influencers, and guests into our events.”

Company description: Bella Hadid has been slowly growing her fragrance brand Orebella since its launch in 2024. Now, with Series A funding from Silas Capital, which has previously invested in beauty brands including Makeup by Mario, Oak Essentials and Ilia, she can scale the line further across categories and markets.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Silas Capital (portfolio includes: Makeup by Mario, YSE Beauty, Dôen).

Company description: NYC-based startup Vetir is pitching itself as an AI luxury shopping app that goes beyond discovery and transactions to act as “a system of record for the wardrobe” for high-value consumers. In practice, this is something of an AI stylist that learns from the data users share with the app, including existing closet items, shopping preferences, as well as their calendar, travel, and purchasing behavior. It’s also building out a business-to-business, CRM-type system for private stylists and luxury clienteling systems, aiming to bring “structure and continuity to what has traditionally been a fragmented, relationship-driven space”.

Funding and round: $5.5 million, Series A.

Investor(s): A consortium of investors across technology and luxury-adjacent family offices.

Company description: Ruka Hair was founded in 2021 by Tendai Moyo and Ugo Agbai, with the mission of supplying hair extensions that are safe, ethical, and good quality. The brand has now received $4.5 million in funding led by Henkel Ventures, the owner of Olaplex and Schwarzkopf. Ruka will be using the investment to scale its business, starting with the launch of US-based operations later this year. The brand has raised $10 million to date and is stocked at Selfridges.

Investor(s): Henkel Ventures, Freedom Trail Capital, Big Issue Invest, Backed VC, Dina Asher-Smith, Knut Alicke, Sophia Dennis, Didier Morais.

Investor comments: “Ruka Hair exemplifies what we look for: founders solving a real problem with genuine commitment, building through community rather than hype,” said Samyr Laine, co-founder and managing partner of Freedom Trail Capital. “Tendai and Ugo built this brand during one of the most challenging periods for consumer businesses, scaled through an authentic community, and are now pioneering biotech innovation that could reshape an entire category.”

Company description: Since founding Anomaly in 2021, Priyanka Chopra Jonas has scaled her haircare brand across North America, the UK, and the Middle East. In the US, the brand is stocked at Target, while in the UK, Superdrug is one of its biggest retailers. Chopra Jonas launched Anomaly with the aim to bring accessibly priced clean and vegan haircare products to the masses. The investment from Reliance will focus on scaling the brand further in India, alongside growing its international presence.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Reliance Retail (portfolio includes: Pahadi Local and Tira).

Investor comments: “Bringing Anomaly into our portfolio marks a strategic step in expanding our basket of new-age, high-growth beauty brands. Anomaly’s strong global positioning, clean formulation, and accessible pricing make it a compelling addition to our ecosystem,” said Isha Ambani, executive director of Reliance Retail Ventures Limited.

Company description: Luxury skincare brand 111Skin was co-founded by husband and wife duo, Dr. Yannis and Eva Alexandridis, in 2012. Their face masks have gone viral since, and in 2025, the brand received a minority investment from Kim Kardashian and Jay Sammons’s private equity firm Skky Partners to help fund its US expansion. Now, the Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) has invested a minority stake that will go toward science-driven innovation.

Funding and round: Minority investment, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): The Estée Lauder Companies (portfolio includes: Le Labo, Jo Malone London, Clinique, La Mer).

Investor comments: “Skincare is entering a new phase, shaped by the convergence of procedures, longevity, and beauty, as consumers increasingly seek products that deliver visible, treatment-inspired results,” said ELC president and CEO Stéphane de La Faverie. “111Skin exemplifies this shift, translating Dr. Alexandrides’s more than 35 years of surgical and aesthetic treatment experience into high-performance skincare inspired by in-clinic treatments and built on clinical insight, next-generation actives, powerful formulas, and proven efficacy.”

Company description: ICCF is a Shanghai and Paris-based premium fashion group that owns Chinese brand Icicle and French brand Carven (acquired in 2018). Kering has acquired a minority stake in ICCF to help develop the former label as part of Kering’s new House of Wonders initiative, which aims to build partnerships that equip emerging luxury houses with strong cultural relevance across markets, categories, and geographies. Icicle will use the funds to expand internationally and into new product categories.

Funding and round: Minority acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Kering (portfolio includes: Gucci, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta).

Investor comments: “This partnership brings together ICCF’s deep understanding of the Chinese luxury ecosystem and cultural landscape with Kering’s longstanding expertise in craftsmanship, operations, and brand development in Europe,” Kering said in a statement. “Through House of Wonders, Kering aims to build long-term value through a disciplined, partnership-driven approach, engaging with brands defined by a distinctive vision, deep authenticity, and global resonance potential.”

Icicle FW26. Photo: Benjamin Cremel/Getty Images

Company description: Grüns is a US-based supplement brand founded in 2023 by Chad Janis, best known for its greens superfood gummy supplement. The brand is digitally-native, with a strong community and a mixed distributed network across retail and direct-to-consumer. The acquisition signals Unilever’s push into the premium wellness category.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever (portfolio includes: Liquid I.V., Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice).

Investor comments: “As a leader and true innovator in the greens supplement category, what sets Grüns apart is its focused portfolio of science-backed products that people genuinely enjoy, trust, and consistently use,” Jostein Solheim, Unilever Wellbeing CEO, said. “This combination of efficacy and experience is powerful, and together we see a significant opportunity to scale the brand within our wellbeing business.”

Investor(s): Softbank, Andreessen Horowitz, D. E. Shaw Ventures, MGX, TPG, Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft, BlackRock, Sequoia Capital, and more.

Company description: Whoop is a wearable tech company known for its fitness tracker that analyzes sleep, recovery, and performance. The company has raised $575 million at a $10.1 billion valuation, and aims to invest the funds into expanding globally, particularly in the US, Europe, the Gulf region, Latin America, and Asia.

Funding and round: $575 million, Series G.

Investor(s): Collaborative Fund (portfolio includes: Reddit, Lyft, TaskRabbit), 2PointZero Group, Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), Mubadala Investment Company, Abbott, Mayo Clinic, Cristiano Ronaldo, LeBron James, Rory McIlroy, Niall Horan.

Investor comments: “Whoop has become one of the most important tools I use to support my long-term health,” said Ronaldo in a statement. “I am proud to participate in this round because I believe in the future we are building together. No other company has created a health platform this powerful that people are proud to wear.”

Company description: Enkei is a Stockholm-based circular material startup founded by CEO Lovisa Sunnerholm (ex-Google and Electrolux) and creative director Miriam Bichsel (a former fashion PR who worked with Hermès and Bottega Veneta). The company has developed ReCeramix™, a circular material made from 90% construction and demolition waste that can be used for architectural surfaces and interior applications, replacing concrete, marble, and terrazzo. With the pre-seed funding, the company will invest in research and development and commercialization opportunities.

Investor(s): Redcap Ventures (portfolio includes: Done, Goodfeed, Eatit), Danish architect Anders Lendager, Lendager Group founder Christina Åqvist, Vinning co-founder and former Tarkett CEO Ulf Mattsson, retail exec Fabian Månsson, bio-materials professor Thomas Granfeldt, materials scientist Daniel Strömberg.

Investor comments: “What Enkei has done in less than two years is what the industry has been talking about for decades. The future of architecture depends on how we rethink materials. Solutions that transform waste into high-value building materials are exactly what the construction industry needs if we want to move toward truly circular buildings,” said Lendager.

Company description: Olaplex was founded in 2014 as a salon-first prestige haircare brand. Slowly becoming the poster child for bond-building hair products, Olaplex has spent recent years navigating slowing sales, as well as legal and consumer scrutiny — including a 2023 lawsuit (which has since been dismissed and disputed) alleging a link between its products and hair loss, scalp irritation, and brittle strands.

Funding and round: Acquisition, $1.4 billion.

Company description: Former professional snowboarder Nima Jalali founded Salt & Stone, a Los Angeles-based premium body care in 2017. The brand has rapidly grown with its minimal packaging and products ranging from deodorants, body wash and oils to facial cleansers and candles. Salt & Stone’s distribution is a growing one as it counts Sephora, Healf, Amazon and Space NK as retail partners. Vogue Business first reported the possibility of a Salt & Stone acquisition back in January.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor comments: “We are thrilled for the opportunity to partner with Salt & Stone, a truly exceptional brand that stands apart in the premium body care and wellness space for its ability to blend experience, performance, and a compelling brand aesthetic,” said ​​David Paresky, a director at Advent. “Nima and the Salt & Stone team have built something rare – a brand with deep consumer loyalty, outstanding products, and an authentic purpose that resonates with today’s consumer all around the world.”

Salt & Stone. Photo: Courtesy of Salt & Stone.

Company description: Huel was founded in 2015 by British entrepreneur Julian Hearn and nutritionist James Collier. Known for its nutritionally complete plant-based meal replacement shakes, Huel hopes to use the investment to expand its position in the competitive supplements category.

Funding and round: Acquisition, €1 billion.

Investor(s): Dandone (portfolio includes: Alpro, Activia, Evian).

Investor comments: “Combining [Huel’s] range and best-in-class digital capabilities with Danone’s global reach and deep nutritional expertise offers exciting opportunities into the new and fast-growing nutritionally complete space, in line with our Renew Danone strategy,” said Dandone CEO Antoine de Saint-Affrique in a statement. “We look forward to learning from one another and unlocking new opportunities and growth for both businesses.”

Company description: Founded in 2020 by Karlee Zhang and Omer Ozener, Hello Klean is a water filtration brand known for its detachable shower heads. The company generated $14.7 million in revenue in 2025, and is projecting $27 million for 2026. Water filter manufacturer Brita has invested a minority investment, with the option to purchase a majority stake over time. Hello Klean plans to use the funds for further product development.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Brita (portfolio includes: Brita, Vivreau, Larq).

Company description: Saks Global has received approval of its five-year business plan by an ad hoc group of the Company’s senior secured bondholders, and has secured access to an additional $300 million of its $1.75 billion in committed capital accordingly. This will provide the company with sufficient liquidity to continue to support operations.

Funding and round: Saks has secured access to an additional $300 million of its $1.75 billion in committed capital.

Company description: Quince, the direct-to-consumer brand that bills itself as a high-quality, accessible alternative for fashion and beyond, has announced a $500 million funding round, resulting in a post-money valuation of $10.1 billion. The funding will support the continued growth and global expansion of Quince’s manufacturer-to-consumer (M2C) operating system, per the release.

Funding and round: $500 million, Series E
