#6679. 3 Ways To Defrost Chicken Without Spreading Salmonella, According To An Expert

Your dinner plans aren't ruined just yet.

Forgetting to take chicken out of the freezer is an all-too-common occurrence that can bring your dinner plans to a screeching halt. To get things back on track, your gut instinct may be to thaw it as quickly as possible. But there are more important things to worry about than a delayed dinner.

Raw poultry can carry Salmonella, so how you handle it matters. Nothing is less appetizing than giving your whole family a foodborne illness.

But before you give up and order takeout, we’re here to help. We chatted with Ellen Steinberg, PhD, RD, LD, and food safety specialist, to find the best (and safest) methods to thaw chicken. Whether you plan ahead or need to defrost it fast, here’s what you should do.

Defrosting chicken isn’t as simple as taking it out of the freezer. Salmonella is real, y’all—according to FoodSafety.gov, roughly 4% of chicken packages at American grocery stores are contaminated with the bacteria. That bacteria can multiply rapidly in the temperature danger zone, between 40°F and 140°F. Translation: Leaving your chicken out on the counter can actually make you sick.

To prevent that, choose the right method and protect the surrounding environment from cross-contamination. Even with supposedly airtight packaging, the plastic may have holes, or chicken juice may transfer from other packages at the grocery store. It’s especially difficult to spot when the meat is frozen, so Steinberg says it’s better to be safe than sorry.

“You should put your [raw] chicken in a roasting pan or a baking sheet so the juices won’t spread,” she says. Everything that touches raw chicken should be thoroughly cleaned with hot, soapy water. If you want to take food safety even further, Steinberg suggests keeping a separate cutting board in a different color that you use exclusively for raw meat. And above all else: Wash your hands!

If you’re not in a rush, thawing chicken in the fridge yields the most consistent results. Because refrigerators should stay at 40°F and below, frozen chicken can gradually defrost without entering the temperature danger zone where bacteria multiply more rapidly.

Because of this, Steinberg says it’s the only USDA-approved thawing method that lets you refreeze raw chicken without cooking it first. “If you end up deciding that you don’t want to cook the chicken or you only want to use half of it, you can place it back in the freezer,” she says. There is a caveat, however: Once your chicken has fully thawed, you should either cook or refreeze it within one to two days.

If you opt for the refrigerator method, keep these safety measures in mind. Beyond keeping your meat contained on a plate or tray, place it on the bottom shelf. If juice drips, it’ll contaminate the fewest ingredients. Steinberg also suggests storing the chicken toward the back of your refrigerator. “The temperature is more consistent, unlike the areas closest to the door,” she says.

If you need to defrost chicken fast, one of the best ways is with cool, running water. Unlike fridge air, water conducts heat much more effectively. Keeping the water moving also helps maintain consistent thawing conditions. But you don't necessarily need to leave the faucet running: The USDA also recommends submerging chicken in cold water and changing it every 30 minutes.

So if cold water thaws meat quickly, would hot water do the job even faster? It might, but the potential food safety risks aren't worth it. "If you thaw chicken under warm or hot water, the outside of the meat can enter the temperature danger zone while the center is still frozen,” Steinberg says.

For the running-water method, place the chicken in leak-proof packaging in a bowl and run cool water (70°F or lower) over it. Thawing times depend on the size and thickness of the meat, but smaller packages may be ready in an hour or less. Once thawed, cook the chicken immediately before considering refreezing it.

The final USDA-approved method involves using your microwave’s defrost setting. While it’s certainly faster than letting meat thaw in the fridge, we suggest relying on this method only if you have no other option.

Steinberg says this technique leaves the least wiggle room for planning your dinner. “You have to cook it immediately,” she says. “You can’t defrost it and then decide to cook two hours later.”

The need to cook immediately is certainly one downside of the microwave method. However, another compelling argument against using the defrost setting is that it can make your chicken taste worse.

Microwaves heat food unevenly, especially with thicker pieces of meat. Some areas can start warming up or even cooking before the center fully thaws. It's not a big deal when reheating leftovers, but it can nearly ruin frozen proteins.

By the time the center is fully defrosted, the outer edges may already be partially cooked. Can you imagine chicken that tastes worse than unseasoned microwaved chicken? We can't.

It’s a safe and fast defrosting method when followed by immediate cooking—but at what cost? So we'd only vouch for this technique if your chicken will end up shredded or submerged in enough sauce to mask the texture.

#6678. Lily James and Lucas Bravo Bring Coordinating Date-Night Style to the Governors Awards Bash

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Lily James shimmied into the Governors Awards in a sparkly silver flapper-style Tamara Ralph dress that dripped with crystal fringe. Silver was a big theme at the event’s starry red carpet, and yet the Rebecca star’s gown stood out for its lively silhouette.

After the Oscars were handed out—honorees includes Glenn Close, Ridley Scott, and Floyd Norman—and the champagne was popped, attendees headed out to the official after-party, held in Los Angeles’s historic Chateau Marmont.

For the occasion, James performed a quick change, trading her electric gown for something a little more subtle (but just as hot): a little black dress.

The mini had a little bow up top, and was layered under an oversize leather blazer for a cool touch. James slipped her legs into sheer black tights and dipped her toes into a pair of Miu Miu’s strappy patent-leather slingbacks with tiny buckles.

She shaded her eyes with skinny black sunglasses, while another Miu Miu staple—the mini Arcadie bag in cherry-red crocodile-embossed calfskin—infused the monochrome look with a welcome pop of color.

Another great part of her look? Her arm candy, beau Lucas Bravo, who was stylish in his own all-black outfit. A classic black T-shirt was layered under a zip-up hoodie and paired with loose trousers. Brown leather loafers broke up the inky color scheme, while chunky black sunglasses with red-orange lenses mirrored James’s pop of red.

The actors began dating just this summer, but as they’re already coordinating looks, we’ll bet the romance is going well.

#6677. Seeing Green on the GQ Men of the Year Red Carpet

The carpet at our annual GQ Men of the Year party may be red, but we’re seeing—dare we say it—Brat green.

Last night, as the stars of our latest MOTY issue gathered at the iconic Chateau Marmont, we noticed a verdant trend emerge on the carpet. Who better to kick things off than two of the most boisterous creatives from our 2026 Breakout Stars crew? First up was actor-comedian Stavros Halkias, who sported a screaming lime green suit by Alan David, a matching Cego silk shirt, and olive-hued Bottega Veneta loafers. Not far behind was Club Kid director-star Jordan Firstman, who also greened out in a full runway look from Anthony Vaccarello’s final menswear collection for Saint Laurent: a boxy, greenish khaki suit with bejeweled buttons, layered over a liquid-silk chartreuse shirt. Both ensembles sure were bright, but ask any color theorist and they’ll probably tell you that wearing green on a red carpet is a surefire way to stand out—they’re opposite of each other on the color wheel for a reason!

The chartreuse looks just kept on coming: the one and only Ice Spice donned a flowing green DSquared2 dress, with matching green eyeshadow (and a curiously hirsute handbag) to boot.

Elsewhere on the carpet, The Bear’s Ayo Edebiri—already a bonafide menswear star—opted for a different but equally striking shade of green. Her sleek striped power suit by London-based designer Connor Ives popped thanks to a kelly green shirt and a contrasting crimson tie. (Edebiri wasn’t the only woman who rocked tailoring on the MOTY carpet this year: model Cara Delevingne, who stars in Firstman’s Club Kid, wore a slouchy-chic black suit by Saint Laurent, while Luciana Damon, wife of cover star Matt, layered a tuxedo-style bolero jacket over her gown.)

If the MOTY red carpet can provide any insights into the year of fashion ahead, we’ll surely be seeing even more green in the months to come. We’re manifesting abundance, in more ways than one.

#6676. Everything You Missed From Inside the Governors Awards

Awards season is officially underway. On Sunday night, Hollywood’s biggest names gathered at the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood for the 17th annual Governors Awards, hosted by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. The star-studded evening celebrated extraordinary achievements and contributions to the film industry, honoring Floyd Norman, Glenn Close, and Ridley Scott, as well as Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, who received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.

After posing for photos on the step-and-repeat, celebrities made their way to the reception just outside the Ray Dolby Ballroom, where the crowd quickly grew shoulder-to-shoulder. Nathan Fielder was among the first to arrive, chatting with fellow guests about his outfit for the evening: a midnight-blue Armani tuxedo. Soon after, a beaming Parker Posey made her entrance in a black lace-and-mesh ensemble, accompanied by Martin McDonagh and Sarah Finn, with whom she recently worked on the new comedy-thriller Wild Horse Nine.

Servers weaved through the sea of guests, offering trays of savory bites, including mini burgers, pierogies, tuna cones, and dates stuffed with goat cheese and pistachios. Close paused to examine the latter, asking one server, “What is that tiny little thing?” Though the legendary actress ultimately passed on the appetizer, the interaction appeared to make the staff member’s day, as the server couldn’t help but smile.

Around 5:45 p.m., an announcement over the loudspeaker signaled for guests to make their way into the ballroom, where dinner would soon be served. Charles Melton lingered at the reception a little longer, chatting with a group that included actress Piper Curda. Inde Navarrette, meanwhile, settled in early, as a waiter poured her a glass of white wine.

Emmy Rossum made her way inside just as the five-minute warning was announced, squeezing past Elizabeth Debicki and Carla Gugino, who were deep in conversation. Among the last to enter the ballroom were husband-and-wife duo Zendaya and Tom Holland, who walked hand in hand.

Upon taking their seats, attendees were greeted with an assortment of appetizers, including smoked salmon oscar matzah, fennel-crusted seared tuna on confit potato, spicy carrot hummus on pumpernickel, and a wagyu carpaccio roll with winter vegetables.

Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was the first to address the room. “Take a look at the five artists we’re honoring here tonight,” she began, sparking a round of applause. “When we think about their extraordinary careers, it’s easy to see the great films, the iconic performances, and the groundbreaking achievements. What we don’t always see are the years of determination behind them, the risks that didn’t pay off, the doors that didn’t open, and the moments when it would have been easier to take a different path. And yet, they kept going, and that is something that should be awarded.”

Following her remarks, dinner was served: pan-roasted chicken with truffle velouté, roasted heirloom carrots, and potato purée. Guests sipped on a selection of wines throughout the evening, including La Clarté de Haut-Brion, Le Dragon de Quintus, and Piper-Heidsieck Champagne.

Norman was the first honoree of the evening, with Mahershala Ali presenting him with an honorary award. “I am so deeply honored to present the first award tonight to a pioneering animator, story artist, and writer who has been creating exceptional work for more than 70 years, the great Floyd Norman,” the two-time Oscar-winning actor said.

During his acceptance speech, Norman reflected on his childhood and the pivotal role his parents played in nurturing his passion for film. “I was a lucky kid because my mom and dad often took me to the movie theater, and those times gave me the education I needed,” he recalled. “In that darkened theatrical classroom, I was just learning the language of film. Somehow, even at that young age, I absorbed the excellent storytelling techniques of lighting, composition, the effective use of sound and music from the Hollywood masters, and seeing on screen what they created in the Hollywood Dream Factory gave me my own dream to become a filmmaker.”

John Malkovich then took the stage to present Close with her honorary award. The actress appeared visibly emotional as she approached the podium, though the mood quickly turned lighthearted when she stumbled over her words while reading from the teleprompter, drawing laughter from the room. “What is that? Wait, put it down the other way. Oh, okay, I got it now!” she exclaimed.

Like Norman, Close looked back on her upbringing, revealing that she was “under the thumb of a restrictive cult” from ages seven to 22. “Don’t look at yourself in the mirror. No flirting. Dress this way. Talk this way,” she recalled of the rules she was expected to follow.

After leaving the cult, Close enrolled at the College of William & Mary as a 22-year-old freshman, and she soon found her calling in the theater department. “It was like water on the desert, the revelation and the deep sense of purpose and fulfillment that started to bud when I stepped onto the stage of Phi Beta Kappa Hall has led me directly to this very moment in this room.”

Next to take the stage was Matt Damon, playfully poking fun at Scott who accepted his award remotely. “Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, Alien: Covenant—these are just three extraordinary Ridley Scott films that he did not cast me in, and I was totally available,” the actor joked, drawing laughter from the room. “All is forgiven though, as I did get to make The Martian with him.”

While accepting his first Oscar, Scott paid a heartfelt tribute to his late brother, Tony. “Now past 80, I’ve thought about those days and moments and it does resonate, it seems like yesterday, both of us sharing our first film together,” he recalled. “I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, and I also accept it for Tony.”

Last but certainly not least, producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler were honored with the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, presented by Julianne Moore—dressed in Bottega Veneta—and Todd Haynes. Before presenting the award, however, the duo had a surprise in store for the audience: a performance by Neil Patrick Harris, who sang “The Origin of Love” from Hedwig and the Angry Inch, a film produced by Vachon and Koffler.

“Tonight’s honorees, your speeches were so incredible,” Vachon began, kicking off their acceptance speech. “We were sitting there going, ‘Oh no! We’re just producers, guys.’” She then turned her attention to her decades-long collaboration with Koffler. “Pam and I have been making movies together for over 30 years. Our longevity and endurance are owed to a few factors: very hard work, plenty of really good luck, and working with the absolute best people, and of course our partnership.”

Koffler then took a moment to look back on their early days working together. “We decided to call ourselves Killer Films. An ethos emerged in those early years, and it has guided the company from day one to champion voices we believe in, stories we love, with a pragmatism that enables them to actually exist.” And just like that, the ceremony came to an end. If the evening was any indication, though, Hollywood is in for a memorable awards season.

#6674. ‘He Needs To Be Layered’: Bond Girl Léa Seydoux Shares the Most Important Traits for the Next 007

What it takes to play James Bond, from the actor who’s played his most influential love interest.

If there’s one Bond girl who has influenced the course of 007 history more than anyone, it’s Dr. Madeleine Swann. Played by French actor Léa Seydoux, who is this month’s ELLE UK cover star, psychotherapist Dr. Swann disrupts the James Bond narrative in a way that no previous lover has done: She challenges his misogyny.

Appearing in the last two films in the series—Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021)—Dr. Swann has a long-term relationship with secret agent 007, eventually telling him that he’s the father of her daughter, making Seydoux’s part in the legendary franchise unique.

Asked whether she would consider a return to the franchise, now under the creative direction of Amazon MGM Studios and without Daniel Craig as 007, the actor said: “I really loved working with Barbara Broccoli and her brother Michael [G. Wilson]. It was one of the best experiences, a pure delight. And I don’t know, it will be different.”

She has already worked with Denis Villeneuve, the director attached to the next Bond film, in Dune: Part Two. “He’s a great choice, let’s see. I’m curious how they will reinvent it. But for me, it will never be the same because it was Barbara’s father who initiated the Bond movies. Now, I don’t know,” she told ELLE. “It became American….I hope they will keep the British spirit.”

As for casting Seydoux in the role, former Bond producer Barbara Broccoli said that her scenes in No Time to Die still move her to tears. “When we were filming the goodbye scene at the Italian train station, Léa approached it with such subtlety—she grasped her stomach to express her pain, but also the secret heartbreak that she was carrying James’s child. It moved me to tears then and continues to move me each time I watch it.”

As for the question of who will play Bond, she won’t be drawn into the speculation. (This was before Robert Pattinson was announced to take on the mantle on November 16.) Seydoux admits that finding the right person to replace Daniel Craig is difficult. “He needs to be layered, you know? And that is something that’s hard to find in young actors.”

Léa Seydoux appears next in Gentle Monster, which begins streaming on Netflix on November 18.

#6671. What Happened To Every Great British Bake Off Winner? Here’s Where They Are Now

From cookbooks to career pivots, the GBBO champs have stayed busy.

Since The Great British Bake Off premiered in 2010, countless talented contestants have shared their passion for puddings, tarts, and everything in between with the world. But only the very best dominated biscuits, perfected their pastries, and showed off their cake skills to get crowned the winner.

But where are those GBBO champs now? From authoring cookbooks to welcoming children, they have kept busy. Some made baking their full-time career, while others stepped away from their ovens. Wherever they ended up, one thing’s for sure: Once a star baker, always a star baker.

“The boy who bakes” paved the way as the first-ever winner of The Great British Bake Off, or The Great British Baking Show as it’s called in the U.S. and Canada. The former debt collector has since focused solely on his writing, cookbooks, and television appearances, often contributing to magazine columns and appearing on shows such as Sunday Brunch and Good Morning America.

Jo Wheatley is one of the few Bake Off champions to have stepped away from their cooking career. Since her season of the show, she has written two cookbooks and even run her own cooking school for a time before retiring and moving to Portugal with her husband. She still shares the occasional recipe on social media and on her blog, but for the most part, keeps it to “sunny snaps & padel in between,” according to her Instagram bio.

Since winning the show, Whaite graduated from Le Cordon Bleu and opened his own cooking school. He also started a bakery and a snack brand. He has appeared on Steph’s Packed Lunch and Strictly Come Dancing, where he finished as the runner-up. He has authored six cookbooks and a memoir, and married his longtime partner in 2024.

The winner of Season 4, Quinn continues her work as a creative consultant, food artist, and designer, and has authored a cookbook. She also holds the Guinness Book of World Records for making the largest Jaffa cake and Jammie Dodgers. She previously hosted a YouTube baking series and creates custom cakes, shares recipes online, and makes occasional media appearances.

Nancy Birtwhistle wasn’t a one-and-done after her 2014 GBBO win—she also participated in The Great British Baking Show: Holidays. Since appearing on the franchise, Birtwhistle has penned a few books on both baking and sustainable living. The GBBO alum also regularly makes appearances on TV and radio shows.

Since dominating Season 6, Nadiya Hussain has become one of the UK’s most prominent celebrity chefs. She has hosted numerous TV shows, including Nadiya’s British Food Adventure, Nadiya Bakes, and The Chronicles of Nadiya, and was even the subject of the documentary Nadiya: Anxiety and Me. The star baker also wrote over 10 cookbooks, plus fiction and children’s books, along with an autobiography.

A year after her 2015 win, Hussain was even commissioned to bake the birthday cake for Queen Elizabeth’s 90th. And in 2020, the chef received an MBE, or Most Excellent Order of the British Empire, for her work in the culinary and broadcasting industry.

Since winning Season 7, Candice Brown has opened her own pub, The Green Man, with her brother in England, as well as Margo’s, a restaurant and deli. She has also penned two cookbooks and written food columns for local newspapers. Brown has also made appearances on numerous other shows, including Dancing On Ice, Loose Women, Pointless Celebrities, and Celebrity Mastermind. She also played a role in the movie Love Sarah.

Since winning Season 8, Faldo has founded her own wedding and specialty cake business: Sophie Faldo Couture Cakes. In addition to her day job, she teaches baking classes in person and online. Plus, she returned to the Bake Off kitchens in 2023 and won The Great Christmas Bake Off.

Things have only gotten busier for Rahul Mandal after his Season 9 win. Since the show, he has released a cookbook and continues baking in his downtime and sharing his creations on social media. He also returned to the franchise and won The Great New Year Bake Off special in 2021. However, the champion still works full-time as a research scientist and engineer at the University of Sheffield. Mandal has also gotten married and had a child.

David Atherton balances his baking with everyday life. The Bake Off winner works as a practice nurse and health advisor by day, and continues his baking pursuits by night, so to speak. Since his win, he has written a series of children’s and adult cookbooks, writes a regular food column for The Guardian, and shares home cooking and baking tips on social media. Additionally, Atherton teamed up with fellow Season 10 baker Michael Chakraverty to launch the Sticky Bun Boys baking and pop culture podcast.

Peter Sawkins made history in 2020 when he became the youngest baker to win GBBO at just 20 years old—and that wasn’t the end of his time on the franchise. Sawkins returned and won The Great New Year’s Bake Off in 2025. Meanwhile, Sawkins has graduated from college and completed pastry training at the Amaury Guichon Pastry Academy. He has also published two cookbooks and frequently shares recipes and baking tutorials online. Additionally, Sawkins works part-time in sports fundraising and plays competitive badminton.

It’s been five years since Giuseppe’s Season 12 win, and he’s upped the ante on his culinary career since. In the past half-decade, Dell’Anno has authored two cookbooks and contributed to a third. He also runs a successful cake business, teaches baking classes in person and online, and frequently shares his baking insights on broadcast television and in food columns. Like some of his fellow winners, he’s also made appearances at local festivals.

Known for recipes featuring bold Malaysian flavors, Syabira Yusoff continues to feed her love of baking by sharing tutorials on social media, hosting online culinary workshops, and judging baking competitions herself. Impressively, she does all this in her free time while continuing her career as a cardiovascular researcher and bioinformatician at King’s College London. Most recently, she announced her engagement to her longtime partner just this past July.

Matty Edgell has stayed busy, both professionally and personally, since winning Season 14. The former high school teacher resigned after the show and now focuses on creating recipes on his website while also sharing baking tutorials on social media. He also tied the knot and welcomed his first child. Edgell publishes a Substack newsletter and has made appearances on TV shows and at local food festivals.

Since her 2024 win, Grasso has kept plenty busy. Not only does the winner post weekly recipes to her Instagram account, but she also released two digital cookbooks earlier this year: Cooking Therapy and Baking Therapy. She has made appearances at local food events such as the Gloucester Quays Food Festival and recently opened up about her bipolar 2 diagnosis.

As the most recent winner of GBBO, Jasmine Mitchell has only a year behind her in the culinary spotlight, but she’s exploded onto the scene with gusto. Since her time on the show, Mitchell has appeared as a guest on numerous talk shows, appeared as a judge on Danish Bake Off, and currently has a cookbook in the works. She’s doing all this while finishing medical school!

#6670. The Data Shows It: The Faux-Fur-Trimmed Coat Is the Coat of the Season

A very specific coat has taken the internet and fashion people alike by storm. Conner Ives’s robe coat looks like a piece pulled from a 1920s opera-house coat check, and everyone from Sienna Miller to Zoë Kravitz has worn iterations of it. First introduced in his fall 2025 collection, it pairs antique silk with reclaimed fox at the lapels and cuffs, and sells for a cool $9,000. And it’s in extremely high demand.

With searches for the designer up 967% on The RealReal, vintage dealers racing to list their versions, and creatives DIYing it at home, it’s safe to call this the coat of the season. While the Ives version might top many of our wish lists (and budgets), its essence is rooted in the feeling of a bygone era—maybe one we’re craving more than ever these days, if the style is any indication.

“The coat taps into a growing appetite for pieces that feel expressive and one of a kind, qualities that have always made vintage compelling,” says Noelle Sciacca, head of fashion at The RealReal. “We’re seeing a real shift toward everyday opulence, rich textures, and a sense of history. The Conner Ives coat captures that mood. It feels glamorous and eccentric but still effortless enough to throw over jeans.”

The proof for demand is in the data. According to Sciacca, searches for fur-trimmed jackets and coats are up 33% year over year, while jacquard searches have increased 60% and tapestry prints have surged 170%. “What’s great is shoppers don’t necessarily need the exact coat to capture the look,” Sciacca says. “They’re exploring vintage and archival pieces across designers and decades, looking for ornate prints, beautiful fabrics, and unexpected details.”

Retailers are also quickly catching on with similar-style coats from Ciao Lucia, Rixo, Dôen, and Maison Essentiele selling out within days of appearing live on their sites. “I had a gut feeling that it [the Taimi Satin Bouquet coat] would be a top seller,” Lucy Akin, founder of Ciao Lucia, shares. “It was validating to not only see it sell out so quickly but also have my entire Instagram feed flooded with these vintage-inspired jackets. They are having a moment, no doubt!”

Stylist Bailey Moon echoes this. “I think there’s a real appetite for clothes that have personality again,” he says. “The Conner Ives coat taps into a sense of nostalgia, but it also feels playful and a little irreverent, which I think is part of its appeal.” That’s also what separates it from the Penny Lane coat. While that style reads bohemian and casual, this one trades suede for silk and leans closer to eveningwear, so the rest of the outfit has less to do.

“Fur and shearling inherently have a sense of drama, so I prefer to let the coat be the centerpiece and keep everything else relatively understated,” Moon shares. “A great pair of trousers, beautiful knitwear, or even a simple dress can make the look feel incredibly modern. I love the contrast of something quite extravagant paired with something very utilitarian.”

Laura Harrier in a short Conner Ives coat

But the appeal extends beyond ornament. Memory and timelessness play a part too. Nour Hammour’s Sima coat was designed after founder Hammour’s grandmother’s coat and the way her grandmother carried herself in it. “It is the balance between exceptional materials, craftsmanship, and a silhouette that will remain relevant long after the season has passed,” shares marketing director Zeina El Zein Hammour. “The quality of the shearling, the depth of the trim, and the way the coat falls on the body are what distinguish a piece that you’ll keep for decades.”

For vintage hounds, it’s also a real marker of the shift away from all-neutral everything that’s dominated for so long. “After years of quiet luxury and minimalism, I think people are ready for a little romance and extravagance,” says Susan Kim of Estella NYC, who sells similar vintage iterations on her site and at vintage fairs.

Kendall Jenner wearing a Conner Ives duster.

Secondhand enthusiast and influencer Katie Casper tried her hand at re-creating the coat using pieces she already owned: a Shanghai Tang silk jacket from her mother-in-law and a removable fur stole from an old Zara coat. “In its simplest terms, the coat is a colorful brocade base with a fur trim,” she says. “Both are easy to source secondhand.” The trickiest part was proportion, since the stole overpowered the jacket; she said she’d choose a narrower one next time.

Whether the style lasts beyond this season is another question. “I fear we may all be a little exhausted by 2027,” Casper muses. But Moon sees it differently. “A beautiful statement coat can live in someone’s wardrobe for years,” he says. “The question is whether you’re buying it because you genuinely love it or because you’ve seen it on everyone else. The best clothes should still feel exciting to wear long after they’ve stopped being the thing everyone is talking about.”

#6669. 15 Best Colognes for Men in 2026, Staff-Tested and Reviewed

In 2026, the best colognes for men go beyond just smelling good, though first things first: They should smell incredible. A great fragrance nowadays tells a story, and if you choose wisely, can become part of your personal lore. I, for one, am a fragrance obsessive and will spritz a cologne at home with nowhere to be, purely for morale. What's more, years of testing and writing about fragrances has taught me just how effortlessly a stellar composition can lift your entire day, whether it’s a mainstream designer release, a niche luxury creation, or something decidedly indie.

My work in the fragrance field has also taught me that while some guys find one signature scent and ride with it for decades; others prefer a variety for different moods, seasons, and days where first impressions matter. To help you figure out where you stand, I tapped the GQ staffers who wear more fragrance in a year than most men do in a lifetime. Collectively, we put old-money classics, cult favorites, and new heat through their atomizers, looking for scents that feel distinctive and deserve repeat wear. The final cut includes a bevy of choices for all occasions, from heritage heavyweights like Acqua di Parma Colonia to future signatures like D.S. & Durga's I Don't Know What. Here's to the sweet smell of success.

Le Labo has no shortage of heavy hitters, from the omnipresent Santal 33 to newer standouts like Eucalyptus 20, but few recent launches have built buzz quite like Thé Matcha 26. Much of its insider appeal lies in its earthy yet fresh, smoky yet subtle, almost Zen-like character. Green fig leads the opening, paired with a calming tea accord, while bitter orange adds a bright bite. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a woodier, herbal edge, with a soft, green haze that runs throughout. A skin scent at heart and undeniably hip, it’s become a modern staple for Le Labo’s more discerning devotees.

Staff Notes: “I’ve been wearing Le Labo’s Thé Matcha for a few years now, and it has become my go-to. As someone who has a hard time finding a scent that doesn't give me a headache or feels too strong throughout the day, it’s one of those rare scents that just works. It has a clean, almost airy quality to it that immediately settles into something effortless and fresh.” —Bowen Fernie, senior visuals editor

Malin+Goetz is one of the few names that began in skincare and went on to make genuinely excellent, indie-cool fragrances, all at very accessible prices. The apothecary vibes run deep, from the formulas to those glass deco bottles that ooze medicine-cabinet chic. The brand's Leather EDP—like my favorite from the line, Cannabis—doesn’t smell exactly like its name. In classic M+G fashion, it plays more of a supporting role here, blended with pepper and clove for a bit of kick. Lily and orchid create a fresh floral heart, while violet adds a velvety depth, all grounded by creamy sandalwood and cedar. And of course, that warm, comforting leather note wears like a Perfecto. It’s a gorgeous spring-ready daily driver, with a grassy floral vibe that plays beautifully against the grain.

Staff Notes: “From the perfect broken-in leather jacket to a leather sofa that's been with you move after move, there's something about the smell of well-loved cowhide that's so damn captivating. Malin+Goetz captured that feeling in a bottle with its Leather EDP. The cologne brings in cedarwood and sandalwood with orchid just to avoid any possibilities of your scent being compared to a vintage store.” —Tyler Chin, associate commerce editor

Is there any cologne more synonymous with men’s cologne, period, than Polo Ralph Lauren? Since 1978, it has helped define what “classically good” smells like and sits firmly planted in the pantheon of modern perfumery. Anything that iconic will have its detractors, but it’s embedded in the culture for a reason, and few colognes today are as recognizable. Even with reformulations over the years, that signature woody aromatic structure still hits, with juniper berry and bergamot up top for brightness, coriander and a blend of herbs bringing spice, touches of florals, and leather for depth—along with that unmistakable pine accord humming throughout. Woody, aromatic, and classic, it’s a cologne guys will always rock.

Staff Notes: “Smelling good is paramount to success as a modern man. (Just ask my close personal friend Ralph Lauren.) Woody, aromatic, and a little spicy, this is a classic scent that's always on top of my dresser.” —Matthew Roberson, staff writer

It’s a household name, a modern icon, and still one of the most sophisticated yet approachable colognes you can wear pretty much anywhere. Created by Chanel’s famed nose, Jacques Polge, more than 15 years ago, Bleu de Chanel remains as singular and versatile today as ever. It opens bright with grapefruit and lemon, sharpened by a hint of fresh mint, before a heart of spicy ginger, warming nutmeg, and heady jasmine. Then comes the MVP lineup of woods: cedar, vetiver, sandalwood, patchouli, and labdanum, all working together in the citrus-spice harmony that defines this blue-hued gem. Flankers have followed, but the OG Bleu de Chanel is inimitable.

Staff Notes: “I keep a travel-sized bottle of this in my Dopp kit at all times. It's classic, great for every season, and super versatile when it comes to occasion—its citrus notes and woody base make it equally good for work dinners, poolside piña coladas, and stoking the fire outside your glamping cabin.” —Ian Burke, senior commerce editor

Baccarat Rouge 540 is now an olfactory cultural landmark. You’ve absolutely smelled this socialite-signature wafting through the night, whether from the backseat of an Uber Black or across a dimly lit dinner table downtown. Some fragrances get so popular they tip into fatigue territory, but 540 earned its status for a reason. First, it comes from one of the most meticulous noses in the game. Second, the scent speaks for itself: an intoxicating, sweet floral amber, with saffron adding a subtle spice, jasmine bringing warmth, and a heavy dose of amberwood creating that signature glowing aura, all balanced by soft woods. Polarizing, yes, but anything that moves the needle tends to follow its own rhythm, and 540 is a modern classic via its own design.

Staff Notes: “Francis Kurkdjian's reputation-making Baccarat Rouge might not be the buzziest scent on the market anymore, but it's definitely the ritziest. If you don't want to smell like a perpetually fapitzed Upper East Side doyenne, you, friend, should reconsider a lot more than just your scent profile.” — Avidan Grossman, senior commerce editor

YSL has no shortage of effortlessly elegant colognes, from more mainstream, accessible options to elevated releases in the Le Vestiaire Des Parfums collection, all infused with that unmistakable YSL panache. On paper, Trench reads as a citrus floral, but in wear, it’s laced with soft, musky undertones that give it an airy, slightly edgy feel. It opens with tangerine and bergamot, layered over heady iris and fresh neroli, before settling into a warm base of musk and cedar. A fig note threads through it all, adding a subtly sweet, verdant hue. Citrusy and floral but grounded in musk, with a slightly funky undertone (the good kind), it’s a chic fragrance you can wear from sun-soaked afternoons in the park straight into date night and out into the cool, tastefully debaucherous night beyond.

Staff Notes: “If you were to bottle the feeling of a perfect Parisian night, it would smell like YSL Trench: heady, sleek, and just a little dangerous.” —Tyler Sparling, contributing market editor

Eau de Minthé is one of the more distinctive entries in Diptyque’s GOAT-level catalog, a cooling blend of mint and patchouli that reads as a fresh, green fougère with a retro ’80s and ’90s edge, albeit very au courant. The mint is fresh and slightly spicy, far from anything toothpaste-adjacent, layered with warm nutmeg, sweet geranium, and a soft, velvety rose. It’s a cologne I wouldn’t have immediately associated with the house, until the drydown, anchored by that signature Diptyque patchouli, brings depth and candle-flickering craftsmanship the brand does so uniquely well. Fresh, aromatic, and with a bit of nostalgia baked in, this is a layered gem to wear for all your mint julep-fueled warm-weather soirées.

Staff Notes: "Diptyque's Eau de Minthé is what I imagine Michelin-level mixologists aspire toward when they're crafting their cocktails. At first sniff, it's garden-fresh floral notes are uplifted with subtle minty notes before settling into deep patchouli notes that give it a well-rounded experience that's equally light and grounding." —Gerald Ortiz, style commerce writer

To me, Tom Ford has four all-timers in his Private Blend canon: Oud Wood, Neroli Portofino, Tuscan Leather, and the sultry tobacco-vanilla duality that is Tobacco Vanille. When this spicy, warm gourmand landed in 2007, it helped redefine what a tobacco fragrance could smell like. The note historically skewed fringe or overtly macho, but Ford, of course, reframed it as chic and decadent, pairing rich tobacco leaf with vanilla, ginger, cocoa, woods, and dried fruits. The signature aroma is plush and addictive, with a near-edible warmth that never tips into excess, as sweet vanilla and spice slowly bloom through the drydown. It’s a masterclass in softening a once-polarizing note into something smooth, inviting, and alluring, and still one of the house’s most widely admired scents today.

Staff Notes: “What's not to love about Tobacco Vanille? It's smooth, smoky, sexy, and just the right amount of sweet. Far better than smoking an actual cigarette—and more luxurious, too.” — Trishna Rikhy, associate social media manager

Musc Ravageur has a devoted following, with fans reaching for this alluring, sultry, spiced gem as both a signature scent and for date nights alike. Released in 2000, it helped usher musk (as a note) into a broader, chicer tier of perfumery. The composition is beautifully layered, opening with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and a heady rose, all resting on a rich base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. Besides being a benchmark for animalic gourmands, it’s one of the most intricately composed scents out there, where, if you read the pyramid, you can pick out each note as it unfolds. We fragrance fanatics love that.

Staff Notes: "This isn't called an icon by accident. I keep coming back to Musc Ravageur year after year. One spray of the warm vanilla, spiced cinnamon, perfectly balanced with clean musk is all it takes for pure chemistry. This is the kind of scent that turns heads." —Reginald Christian, commerce director

London-based Perfumer H has carved out its own unique path, from its apothecary-meets-indie-meets-luxury vibe to its often one-word, subtle creations that smell distinctive yet approachable. Ink is a case in point. As a self-proclaimed bookworm, I was already sold on its inspiration: late nights spent in dimly lit libraries. But the scent itself is an intriguing study, weaving together woods, papyrus (because paper, of course), heady rose, spice, warm ambers, and an incense-like, meditative quality. The result is an addictive, page-turning woody floral composition that feels both cerebral and wearable, the kind of fragrance you rock when you're quite possibly the coolest dude in the room—and likely the most well-read, too.

Staff Notes: “Perfumer H pretty much had me at their tagline: Making Air Visible. But then I smelled Ink, and was completely seduced. It transports me to lamp-lit reading rooms and old-world ateliers. And even better, because it's so light, I can apply it multiple times a day.” —Louis Cheslaw, contributing commerce editor

Well before skin scents became a thing, the indie aromatic heavyweights at D.S. & Durga dropped their now cult-classic I Don’t Know What Eau de Parfum in the late 2010s. It is less a traditional fragrance and more of an enhancer (though for many, it is the main aromatic event). The polar opposite of beast-mode projection, subtlety is its byword, with a verdant, woody air scent you lean in to experience rather than one that announces itself across a room. Iso E Super, a versatile synthetic aroma chemical known for its longevity and velvety skin-like texture, does most of the heavy, or rather light, lifting, blended with bergamot, vetiver, and sandalwood to create one of the best fresh skin scents of all time. Wear it on its own or use it to boost and layer with other fragrances. I don’t know what else to say; it all works.

Staff Notes: “I Don’t Know What has a gentle and clean scent that feels like a whisper compared to more bombastic fragrances out there. The light citrusy hit of bergamot is exactly what I need when layering scents during the warmer parts of the year.” —Jordan Bowman, commerce editor

One of the genre’s most renowned reference vetivers, this Guerlain classic has influenced not just every vetiver cologne, but many fragrances today, period. The composition is less the smoky, rooty side of the note and more early-morning, dewy freshness, clean and crisp, with just enough (good dirty) earthiness underneath to keep it interesting. Citrus and spice lift the opening before it settles into a grassy core, rounded out by touches of tobacco and woods. More than any grand concept, it smells like stepping outside early in the morning, when everything still feels a little cool, damp, and alive. With longevity and that timeless cologne feel, it has remained a benchmark since its 1950 debut and a signature scent for so many.

Staff Notes: “This bottle has been in my rotation for a few years, and it’s a benchmark for anyone into fresh, verdant scents. To my nose, it’s always smelled of drinking a Negroni in a five-star hotel room, or someplace equally polished. I spritz it particularly in the colder months whenever I’m set to meet new people, because I find it's an easy way to make a good first impression.” —Michael Nolledo, commerce director

So many folks whose taste I admire wear Colonia. Endlessly polished and easy to wear, it’s about as close as it gets to a perfect daily driver. First introduced in 1916, the Italian icon still feels as relevant today as it did over a century ago, built on that signature blend of citrus, herbs, and woods, wearing its subtlety and old-world refinement on its (freshly pressed) sleeve. The opening is citrus crisp, before settling into herbaceous notes of lavender, rosemary, and vetiver over a smooth base of patchouli, sandalwood, and soft amber warmth. It carries that classic barbershop fougère-meets-Italian-citrus-grove energy, a cologne your dad (and his dad) wore to work and date nights alike—but that smells just as fresh on you today.

Staff Notes: “'It's hard to pick the perfect cologne for the office’ is something I might say if I'd never smelled this bottle of Acqua di Parma. It smells like biting into a sexy tangerine, but in an inoffensive way that won't raise any eyebrows in your desk clump." —Doug Guida, social producer

Every exemplary fragrance house has a defining undercurrent. With Aesop (who's just as well known for its scents as its skincare), it's a botanical, earthy, elevated thread running through those amber-hued bottles. Rōzu Eau de Parfum is a woody, aromatic, rose-forward composition, not of the sweet or traditional variety, but for those who appreciate richer, headier takes. Rose, alongside iris, is one of my favorite floral notes, and here it's handled with nuance, pairing the dewy, velvety accord with a lift of citrus, then grounding it with sandalwood for creaminess, guaiac wood for incense-leaning flourishes, and vetiver for earthiness. A jasmine accord adds depth to the green, earthy rose aroma—another indie homerun from the Aussie house.

Staff Notes: “I thought I wasn’t a rose-cologne person, but then Aesop mixed in some shiso and jasmine, and it was love at first whiff. Rōzu (the Japanese pronunciation of the English word “rose”), is my go-to when I want a unisex scent that’ll last just a bit longer than the work day, because I don’t want to be That Cologne Wearer at the gym.” —Mari Herrema, marketing and production manager

Perhaps no cologne is as referenced, memed, reviewed, and well-known in modern mainstream fragrance culture as Sauvage. The line can get a little confusing, but it all comes back to a core DNA built on citrus, pepper, and ambroxan, just pushed in different directions. The EDT is ultra-fresh, the EDP adds warmth, and the Parfum goes denser. Then there’s Elixir, the darker, spicier, more aromatic outlier. It’s my favorite of the group, leaning into evening territory with nutmeg and cinnamon bringing gourmand warmth, grapefruit adding lift, and classic lavender giving it that fougère backbone, all resting on a heady base of amber, patchouli, sandalwood, and a subtly sweet licorice accord. Elixir is the refined, yet still slightly mischievous side of Sauvage—spicy, warm, fresh, and it smells good on pretty much everyone.

Staff Notes: “I was gifted a bottle of Dior Sauvage, I think, to give to a man in my life. But I love men's colognes so I decided to keep it for myself. When winter rolled around, I gave it a try and I noticed pretty immediately that the scent had pull. (I got the most interest from an Uber driver who was terribly into my fragrance until I told him it wasn't for women.) Somehow it gave me that fresh-out-of-the-shower burst of energy while also smelling woody, warm, and sexy—perfect for cooler days. I'm happy I didn't give it away.” —Savannah Sobrevilla, associate editor

The fragrances above are all GQ staffer favorites, and I worked closely with the team to bring to life what makes each one worthy of a spot in your olfactory arsenal. Of course, scent is wildly subjective. One person's all-time favorite daily driver might leave someone else scrunching their nose. Tomato, tomahto. That's part of the fun, after all. No universal crowd-pleaser exists, and what smells incredible on one guy might not work for the next.

Now, here's where I get to shine a light on a few personal favorites. From modern classics to under-the-radar niche gems and newer fumes, these are the colognes I love right now, along with a few I think deserve more attention, spanning a range of price points. Consider this a little extra olfactory inspiration, courtesy of yours truly.

I've smelled pretty much everything indie-luxe stalwart Byredo has put out over the years (including the new, fantastic Future Memories), but it wasn't until recently that I finally got my nose on Oud Immortel. It brings together just about every cold-weather note I adore, from oud and smoky incense to earthy patchouli, moss, and tobacco, weaving them into something sultry and almost decadent. But there's also that signature Byredo airiness, an almost skin-scent-like softness that keeps it from feeling too dense or overpowering.

When I first experienced Terre d'Hermès years ago, it immediately became a staple in my rotation. It's one of the best designer colognes ever, and I was, and still am, obsessed with its woody, citrusy elegance. But while the original is best suited to cooler months, with Eau Intense Vétiver, you've got an equally chic, warm-weather counterpart.

French grooming favorite Horace knows how to make fragrances that smell like they should cost far more. Inspired by Freddie Mercury's legendary 41st birthday bash at Ibiza's Pikes Hotel in 1987, this is one intriguing aromatic. The name sounds summery, but to my nose, it's more like a winter holiday celebration, with crisp fir balsam and cypress lending an evergreen character.

I’ve been intrigued by New York-based Vilhelm Parfumerie for years, right down to those distinctive bottles shaped like miniature decanters, and Morning Chess is so, so smooth. It’s a blend of citrus and amber you don’t come across often: fresh and bright on the surface, just like the morning, but a few swift chess moves later, it settles into a regal, leathery warmth with an earthy undercurrent. Checkmate.

I’m a big fan of buzzy Brooklyn house Rite of Way, as all three (yes, just three) of its fragrances are so wonderfully indie and cool. I’m normally not one for aquatics, but its inaugural scent, Outer Realm, won me over by pairing citrus and marine notes with incense to create a scent that’s anything but banal. Citron and grapefruit bring a sharp, juicy brightness, while sea spray and lotus lend an airy, almost otherworldly quality. Then, as it settles, amber emerges, giving the composition a warmth you don't typically associate with aquatics.

Quentin Bisch is one of the most renowned and daring perfumers working today, and to my nose, he has a way with woods, giving them a richness and depth that's become a calling card. His Bois Impérial for Essential Parfums, a niche house known for making high-quality fragrances more accessible, has become a sensation on fragrance forums, and for good reason. Built around Akigalawood, a patchouli-derived ingredient with a rich woody character, it has a spicy, peppery bite, while an invigorating freshness keeps it from veering too heavy.

Los Angeles–based Perfumehead’s exemplary Canadian Tuxedo reminds me of my childhood on Long Beach Island: Evening light dancing off the driftwood, when everything felt quiet, introspective, and creatively stirring. On paper, it sits in the amber family, but it wears like a meeting of resinous woods and coastal air, lifted by bitter orange leaf and coriander. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a warm, herbal quality with a touch of spice and a soft, musky finish that feels almost windswept.

I respect the citrus fragrance family immensely, but as a leading note, it’s never been my everyday go-to. L’Or de Louis completely reframed it for me: a citrus shaped by smoke and gourmand tones that’s become a fixture in my olfactory arsenal. Aromatic indie heavyweights Arquiste have a knack for weaving history into their fragrances, and this one takes us to Louis XIV’s Versailles, where bonfires burned near citrus trees at the Grand Orangery. The gold flecks in the bottle are another nod to its grandiose inspiration, resembling, to me, little flickers of fire suspended in the glass.

I recently watched a podcast where Sarah Sherman lamented that she could no longer get her hands on Santa Maria Novella's Patchouli. That's the kind of attachment people develop to the centuries-old Florentine house, helped also by its gorgeous bottles. I like Opoponax: a honeyed resin with a smoky, incense-like quality. Think monks in cloisters, holy water, dimly lit chapels, and quiet garden courtyards.

Even as Icelandic house Fischersund gains serious attention stateside, it still feels like the cool kid in the room, with a noir-leaning sensibility and music and art woven into its indie DNA. I adore No. 23, the flagship scent, which opens dark and smoky, almost charred, before softening into resinous woods, spice, and a hint of sweet citrus with a faint animalic undercurrent.

It's not often I get to shine a light on a gem in Creed's storied catalog that isn't one of its many heavy hitters, but Bois du Portugal is a bit of a slept-on classic that currently has me hooked. An old-school gentleman's fougère, it's fresh, woody, spicy, and above all aromatic, built from little more than bergamot, a hefty dose of lavender, and a blend of woods and patchouli—proof that a few top-quality elements, blended exceptionally well, can speak volumes. Created in 1987, it still smells every bit as relevant today.

Iberian Leather isn't for beginners; it's the kind of scent you have to vibe with to appreciate its artistry and complexity. A richly layered fragrance, it feels like wandering through a damp, historic castle as aged wood, worn leather, and the scent of nearby flower beds wafts through the night air. And the bottle is flat-out stunning, too, looking like something straight out of Game of Thrones.

Ever wondered about the difference between an “EDT” and an “EDP?” It's not actually all that complicated. The primary differentiator comes down to the percentage of perfumed oils used in the product, which dictates how brands classify their scents. These days, we tend to treat “cologne” as a catchall term for any men’s fragrance, but technically speaking, the term is just one of many you should know about. These are the rest.

The classifications above aren't an exact science, of course, but the concentration levels they allude to are a solid indicator of where to set your expectations, and how much a fragrance will cost.

Colognes right now have more personality than ever, and more and more gentlemen are moving beyond the one-bottle approach. Plenty of guys still swear by a signature scent, but many are building rotations based on budget, mood, and setting. As Jake Levy and Matt Belanger, founders of NYC fragrance shop Stéle, told us, “Today folks want variety: one to go out, one to go to work, one for date night, and even one to start a conversation.”

If you’re starting from scratch, keep it simple: start with two bottles—one clean, versatile daily driver and one with a little more edge for nights out. From there, add by season or occasion, like say, something fresh and citrusy for warm weather, something woody or spicy for when the temps drop.

Keep this in mind, too: classic fragrance families like citrus, woods, gourmand, and floral will always have a place, but modern perfumery is more wide-open than ever. As Carlos Huber of Arquiste puts it, if you love smoky oud or animalic leather, there’s no reason it can’t be your best cologne. Wear what fits your aura, not your algorithm.

As one of GQ’s regular fragrance writers, I’ve spent years testing colognes and reporting on the category, while the wider shopping team has spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about what deserves space on a shelf. Together, we cast a wide net, considering household names, indie favorites, heritage heavyweights, and artisanal imprints.

Because not every guy wears cologne the same way, or for the same reasons, we pay close attention to context and budget. We test scents on skin over full days of wear, tracking how they opened, dried down, projected, and lasted over time. Some needed to work at the office, others on date nights, others as an everyday signature. Each winning pick was judged on scent quality, longevity, versatility, and price, along with the simplest test of all: whether we actually wanted to keep spraying it.

The result is a list that reflects a range of tastes, occasions, and price points—from tried-and-true stalwarts to modern disruptors, affordable go-tos to wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) flexes.

#6667. Sonic Is Bringing Back 10 Iconic ’80s & ’90s Toys—And Yes, There’s A Furby

Good luck convincing adults these are just for kids.

Tell the Happy Meal to move over—Sonic's Wacky Pack is here to steal its thunder. The kids' meal comes with a choice of entree, side, and drink, plus a toy. Past collections have included everything from Hello Kitty to Hot Wheels to Batman. Now, however, Sonic has teamed up with toy giant Hasbro to bring 10 throwback collectibles to its Wacky Packs.

The new collection is available now through the end of January 2027 at participating locations, while supplies last, and it's sure to get plenty of '80s and '90s kids excited.

And hold onto your scrunchies, because these toys might have you Skippin' It straight to Sonic the second they drop. The lineup includes pink and yellow Furbies with eyes that appear to blink, pink and yellow mini NERF Super Soakers, and My Little Pony figures featuring Applejack and Blossom. There are also Transformers figures of Megatron and Optimus Prime with glowing eyes, plus Littlest Pet Shop cat and dog leash spoons with removable figures.

Each Wacky Pack comes with one toy, and the design may vary depending on what's available.

Fans wasted no time reacting to the collection on Instagram. “OH MY F*****G GOD,” one person wrote, while another commented, “Guess I'm going to Sonic again.”

The Littlest Pet Shop spoons got plenty of attention, too. “Need 2 billion of those spoons please,” one user wrote, while another commented, “Give me the LPs spoons idc if u just called them retro.”

The love wasn't limited to one toy either, as another future customer said they “WILL be at sonic to get the ponies.”

If nostalgia is your jam, you'll want to get in line to get your hands on one—or all—of these new toys, whether you're a kid or not.

#6665. Everything You Need to Know About the 2027 Grammy Awards

Believe it or not, the 2027 Grammy Awards are just around the corner. With the nominees now announced—and including the likes of Taylor Swift, Rosalía, Ariana Grande, Madonna, Raye, Olivia Dean, Tinashe, and Cardi B—it’s officially time to start counting down to the ceremony.

Below, find everything we know so far about the 2027 Grammys.

The 69th Annual Grammy Awards will take place on Sunday, February 7, 2027.

The 2027 Grammys will be held at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, just as they were in 2026.

The main Grammys telecast will air live on ABC (and stream on Disney+ and Hulu) from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. PST.

Well, we know who it won’t be: after six consecutive stints as host, Trevor Noah took the Grammys stage for the final time earlier this year. As for who will take his place? That’s still yet to be announced.

Raye led the awards ceremony with a whopping 11 nominations, closely followed by Rosalía with nine, Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, and Phoebe Bridgers with seven apiece, and Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas, and Olivia Dean with six each.

The official lineup for the 2027 Grammys hasn’t been announced yet—but watch this space!

#6664. GQ’s Men of the Year Dinner May Have Found the Next James Bond

Cocktail hour was drawing to a close; the traditional pre-party dinner for the 31st edition of GQ’s legendary Men of the Year event, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, was about to kick off. GQ’s Designer of the Year, Celine’s Michael Rider, and our Director of the Year, Denis Villeneuve, were already posted up inside the Chateau Marmont’s lobby lounge; the guests lingering just past the entrance included Odysseus himself, Matt Damon, building with his Ocean’s partner-in-crime Don Cheadle before pivoting to greet Chris Rock—like Damon, one of GQ’s three Men of the Year issue cover stars. (Andrew Garfield, subject of that third cover, had rolled in a few minutes earlier, resplendently coiffed, immediately gathering his After the Hunt co-star Ayo Edebiri and director Luca Guadagnino into a reunion hug.)

But among the Men of the Year veterans in attendance—like Rock, who scored his first MOTY cover in 1999, circa Bigger and Blacker—there were also plenty of first-timers from the new class of news-makers and paradigm-shakers celebrated in GQ’s 2026 Breakouts portfolio. And that varied mix—of longtime icons and undeniable up-and-comers, from Owen Thiele and Inde Navarette to I Play Rocky’s Anthony Ippolito and electro-rock duo Fcukers—made for a veritable particle accelerator of improbable collisions.

Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg in deep confab with Tinashe. Tony’s Stavros Halkias in an across-the-table comedy summit with Chris Rock. Journalist Pablo Torre, whose reporting on Kawhi Leonard and the LA Clippers salary-cap shenanigans shook the NBA, engrossed in conversation with GQ’s own Zach Baron and Villeneuve, who’d just signed off on the prints—for real this time—for his third and final Dune movie, soon to shake the walls of nearly every IMAX theater on Earth.

And Villeneuve wasn’t the only auteur on hand: Between the Dune mastermind, Misty Green writer/director/star Rock, Club Kid’s similarly slashed Jordan Firstman, the La Bola Negra writer-directors jointly known as Los Javis (Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi) and Guadagnino, who upon arriving had almost immediately located a cinematically moody lamplit corner to hold court in, the Chateau’s lobby was, quipped GQ Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi, “an incredible room to be an out-of-work actor in.”

Because journalism doesn’t take a night off—not even GQ’s biggest night—Baidawi also tried, during his opening remarks, to pry some info regarding the identity of the new James Bond (off the record, just between us) out of Villeneuve.

As the director politely demurred—hey, we had to try—another guest piped up from across the table. “Wait,” said Matt Damon, as Baidawi passed the former superspy the mic. “I have a question. Just a thought experiment. What if James Bond were older? And American?” (In the unlikely event that Damon just booked a second iconic-superspy role, you heard it here first.)

Toast time was upon us: Rosalind Eleazar, raising a glass to Chris Rock, recalled her Zoom audition with Rock for Misty Green, which was followed in short order by a missed call from an American number and the two-word text message that would change her life: “Chris Rock.” (That’s right—when Chris Rock calls you from an unknown number and gets your voice mail, he follows up with a text that just says “Chris Rock,” an absolute power-move that is, unfortunately, hard to replicate by the rest of us.)

“Thinking I was being rather witty, I replied, ‘Rosalind Eleazar,’” Eleazar said. “I waited eagerly for his response and—not so much as a laughing emoji. And I quickly realized that I am communicating with one of the funniest people on the planet and I should probably just leave the funny to him.”

Eleazar recalled Rock telling her on set, My movie—your character, giving her the freedom to discover Misty on her own. “And that’s a rare gift,” she said, “and one that I will always be grateful for.”

“Thank you, Rosalind,” Rock said. “The check will be there in the morning.”

Ayo Edebiri began by saluting “my dear friend, one of my favorite people in the world, one of the best actors ever, and a little bit of a role model to me if I’m being honest: Robert Pattinson.” She paused as the crowd fell out laughing. “Andrew! Andrew Garfield. I’m so sorry. This is a different speech for a different guy.”

“You never know what you’re going to get when you work with somebody,” Edebiri noted, but said the resolutely “normal” Garfield had put her immediately at ease on After the Hunt, making it “safe to be unsafe” in difficult scenes. “And, on that movie especially, we had tough stuff to do,” she said. “We were not nice to each other. Some of the boys these days, on Method, you never know.”

“If you ever see him in public,” Edebiri continued, “don't try any small talk with this man. Just don't do it. He's medically allergic to small talk. You get very deep, very fast. You will end up talking about esoteric poetry or the nature of masculinity in the modern world or just water, like the power and the mystery of water.” (This we can confirm.)

“I just love you so, so dearly,” Garfield responded, “and I hope we can be in each other's lives forever.”

And with that moment of open-hearted sincerity out of the way, it was time for Damon to hear from frenemy Jimmy Kimmel, who fired off weapons-grade roast jokes. “I fought for the First Amendment this year,” Kimmel said. “You fought a puppet cyclops.”

Damon, in response, mostly took the high road, offering up praise (for Edebiri’s speech) before getting the last word. “In closing, I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place. I’ve never invited him anywhere, and I never will. He is a horrible human being. And I thank you all for being here.” ✦

#6663. In Being Heumann, Ruth Madeley Brings to Life One of America’s Most Important Disability Activists

The film, based on the Judy Heumann memoir of the same name, is now streaming on AppleTV

Being Heumann, the new film about disability activist Judy Heumann, played by Ruth Madeley, opens with one of those classic New York City street montages: the morning rush hour commute, a close-up of feet pounding the sidewalk, yellow cabs buzzing by. Then, a wheelchair speeding down a bumpy road, splashing in puddles. Judy, a woman riding a motorized wheelchair in the middle of the road, weaves between traffic and over steaming manholes. She crosses the street, but there are no ramps on the sidewalk, so she gets back on the road, zig-zagging between drivers yelling at her to get out of the way. When a giant city bus gets behind her and threateningly honks its horn, Judy simply raises her right hand, gives the driver the middle finger, and continues on her way unfazed. We are barely three minutes into the film.

Written and directed by Sián Heder, whose previous film Coda, won Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay at the 2022 Academy Awards, Being Heumann chronicles the 504 Sit-In, which is the longest non-violent occupation of a federal building in US history which led to the passing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act which, among other things, made it illegal to discriminate on the basis of disability, and also called for making public buildings and transportation accessible, and would set the basis for the American with Disabilities act, 1990’s landmark civil rights legislation.

“So often, disabled characters in particular—and especially women—are very softly introduced,” says Madeley a few days before the movie debuts on AppleTV+. “[But] This is who Judy is. She was doing this every day. You’re completely captivated by, ‘Oh my god, where is this woman going?’ I remember her brother said there were so many times she nearly got hit by a car.” Judy’s unapologetic attitude is the driving force behind her activist group—even if it sometimes puts her at odds with others.

There is a popular saying on social media, “Well-behaved women rarely make history,” and yet so often women—even activists, or especially activists—need to fit into neat preconceived notions of how to respectfully ask instead of demand for change. “[Judy] wasn’t always likable. She was an asshole sometimes, she was stubborn and she could railroad people sometimes… but I think that’s what makes her so compelling,” says Madeley. “The audience understands where she’s coming from because she had years of being told ‘No, you can’t go to school,’ ‘No, you can’t be a teacher,’ ‘You can’t come in here, you’re a fire hazard’... just years of injustice. And she was done with it. She was tired of it.” Madeley adds, “I was so excited that Sián and Rebekah [Tausig, who co-wrote the script], didn’t round off Judy’s edges because she was a complex person. She was messy, and I love playing a messy, complicated woman.”

Being Heumann tells the story of one of the most important leaders of disability rights in American history, and has already broken ground for its diverse cast of actors who are disabled for its main roles. Still, Madeley rejects its purpose as a mere “history lesson.” “This is what people want to go to the movies to see. They want to laugh, they want to cry, they want to go on a ride with a bunch of people storming a building when they have absolutely no idea what they’re doing,” she explains. The movie does in fact have the ebullience of the classic “us against the world” trope (my mind goes to Empire Records, a personal favorite, except with higher stakes)—as the activists hunker down inside the Federal Building in San Francisco, they turn the space into a temporary utopia: the Black Panthers bring them food and weed and they host classes and panels on topics like sexuality. (In one of the best scenes in the movie, as Judy is getting intimate with Jim Pechin, her fellow activist who’s been flirting with her since the beginning of the movie, she says, “I’m going to tell you what I want and you’re going to do as I say.” What other movie has ever displayed this level of control and empowerment in a sex scene? “The complexity and the different nuances of that scene really interested me, and I’d never seen anything like that on screen before,” Madeley explains.)

Another scene that broke ground on how we’ve seen disability on film came early on, when Judy is in bed waiting for her home attendant, who is running late, and Judy really has to go to the bathroom. “Movement fascinates me on screen, it always has,” Madeley reveals. “What really interested me was how Judy was so quick and forever moving and busy when she was in her chair, like she is free in her chair and then the stark contrast to how vulnerable and dependent on other people when she’s out of her chair. That scene is really poignant because Sián didn’t make it choppy, she wanted it to be in real time, and she wanted the audience to feel the rigamarole. Judy has no core strength, so she has to be balanced, she has to move the plates on her wheelchair, then she’s transferred, then she has to move the plates back, take the locks off… There are all these different stages just to be able to use the bathroom.” She adds, “Honoring Judy’s physicality was just as important to me as honoring all the different layers of her personality.”

Madeley, who also portrayed British disability rights advocate Barbara Lisicki (in the BBC film Then Barbara Met Alan), wants people to have fun while watching Being Heumann. That said, she also hopes they come away with “a better understanding of the physical world around them.” She continues, “Every time I go down a curb cut, I’m like, ‘Thanks, Judy.’ That curb cut wasn’t just there, it didn’t just appear. It was fought for.”

#6662. McDonald’s Just Brought Some Of Its Most Popular International Dishes To The U.S.

Why let other countries have all the fun?

You can find a McDonald's in over 100 countries, each offering unique international menu items. But you may not know that you can try some of them in the States—no passport required.

The restaurant at McDonald's Chicago headquarters has featured a special rotating menu of global favorites since opening in 2018. Its newest lineup has officially dropped, and it includes some dishes you don't want to miss.

The menu currently features two sandwiches. The first is Costa Rica's Mushroom Deluxe McCrispy, which comes with a crispy chicken fillet, cooked mushrooms, Swiss cheese, mayo, and crispy onions and garlic. You can also order a Chili Cheese McDouble from Germany that upgrades the classic burger with pickled jalapeños and a hot chili cheese sauce.

The Global Favorites menu wouldn't be complete without McNuggets, either. McDonald's is currently offering a version from Japan with spicy garlic black pepper seasoning.

Instead of the chain's classic fries, you can round out your global meal with Malaysian Twister Fries—otherwise known as curly fries. And to top it all off, there's a Strawberry Cheesecake McFlurry from Canada. (If there's any menu item that deserves a nationwide American debut, it's this one.)

Fast food fans reacted to the new menu with a combination of excitement and serious FOMO. "I'm moving to Chicago just to eat at the HQ full time," one Instagram user wrote. On X, another fan added, "Garlic black pepper nudges? You have my attention."

If you want to try any of these menu items for yourself, you'll have to visit the McDonald's headquarters restaurant at 1035 W. Randolph Street in Chicago. The Global Favorites menu rotates regularly, so don't put off your trip for too long.
