#6658. Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Beauty mogul Kylie Jenner and actor Timothée Chalamet sparked a romance in 2023, shortly after Jenner split with the father of her two children, Travis Scott. She and Scott had an on-again-off-again relationship for a few years and now co-parent their daughter, Stormi, and son Aire.

While Chalamet and Jenner are an unexpected couple to fans, they’ve been together for years. Chalamet even gave Jenner a public declaration of love at the 2026 Critics Choice Awards, saying in his acceptance speech, “I’ll just say thank you to my partner of three years. Thank you for our foundation. I love you. I couldn’t do this without you. Thank you from the bottom of my heart.”

Here’s everything we know about their love story so far.

On January 25, Jenner and Chalamet were seen enjoying one another’s company at Paris Fashion Week during the Jean Paul Gaultier show. This was allegedly their first meeting, and a video of them laughing together surfaced on social media once rumors started circulating that they were more than friends.

TMZ released pics of Jenner’s black Range Rover parked outside Chalamet’s Beverly Hills home amid rumors the two stars were dating.

On April 14, a source told People that the pair had been “hanging out and getting to know each other.”

A few days later, another source told Entertainment Tonight that they were officially dating, but things were “not serious.”

“They are keeping things casual at this point,” the insider explained. “It’s not serious, but Kylie is enjoying hanging out with Timothée and seeing where it goes. It’s been really fun for her because it feels a lot different than her past relationships. It’s new and exciting for Kylie, and she’s having a lot of fun.”

They added, “Kylie decided she didn’t want to make things public with Timothée this past weekend at Coachella and really just wanted to chill and have fun with her friends.”

Another insider told People that the two “hang out every week,” but it’s “not serious.”

“She is getting to know him,” the source added. “Kylie is having fun. After years of back and forth with Travis [Scott, her ex-boyfriend and father of her two children], she just wants to date without any pressure.”

In May, a source told Entertainment Tonight that the new couple was trying to keep things quiet. They're “casually seeing each other but are trying to keep it low-key,” the source said.

“They are becoming more comfortable with each other, but Kylie wants to take things day by day and see where it goes,” they added. “Her family thinks it’s great that Kylie is doing her thing, and they are supportive.”

The source continued, “Timothée loves that Kylie is such a hands-on mom and a boss. He appreciates her confidence and thinks she’s incredibly beautiful.”

Jenner’s ex Travis Scott was also reportedly disturbed by their connection.

“Travis is not thrilled about Kylie moving on, but they are still cordial and focused on co-parenting and being the best parents they can be,” the insider said.

In late May, Jenner’s black Range Rover SVA was seen outside Timothée Chalamet’s mansion in Beverly Hills, California. It stopped off early in the morning then left with a security detail.

On Thursday, June 1, the couple was seen outside Chalamet’s Beverly Hills home and then out for lunch wearing matching tie-dye shirts.

In July, Scott seemed to comment on Jenner’s relationship with Chalamet on his new album Utopia. On a track called “Meltdown,” Scott appears to make a reference to Chalamet’s role in the new movie Wonka, a take on the classic novel Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory. He raps:

Following false early August tabloid breakup rumors, TMZ and Entertainment Tonight both reported that Jenner and Chalamet’s romance was still going strong.

A source told Entertainment Tonight on August 16, “Kylie and Timothée are still seeing each other when they can. Kylie’s busy with work and traveling a lot, but they make time for each other when it works and both like each other. They’re keeping things low key and chill for now, but get along great and have fun together.”

On September 4, Jenner and Chalamet made their public debut at Beyoncé’s concert. They were filmed keeping close to each other and talking during the show.

TMZ obtained video of them kissing there in the first PDA sighting.

Just a few days later, on Friday, September 8, the new couple was seen at a New York Fashion Week dinner for the launch of Haider Ackermann’s beauty collaboration with Augustinus Bader, Vogue reported. Jenner was Chalamet’s plus one. Also attending were Jared Leto, Oscar Isaac, Sofia Coppola, and Amelia Gray Hamlin. In a video on TikTok, Jenner is sitting beside Chalamet.

The couple went on to attend the US Open together. They were seen kissing there on September 10.

On September 19, a source spoke to Entertainment Tonight about how Jenner feels really comfortable dating Chalamet. The insider explained that Jenner and Chalamet went public at Beyoncé’s concert on September 4 “because she is confident and secure in their relationship. [She] feels like she can be herself with him [and] really likes that.”

Jenner and Chalamet “also connect on a deep level,” the source said, adding that “Timothée is also a family man, and they relate to each other about that. Kylie’s friends and family think Timothée is great and love seeing her happy.”

On September 21, ELLE Mexico captured photos of Jenner at Prada’s fashion show with her Timothée Chalamet lock screen visible on her iPhone. Although it was likely unintentional, it marked the first little hint Jenner gave herself of Chalamet’s place in her life.

And on September 25, Chalamet and Jenner were photographed together again, this time in Paris. The pair was seen holding hands while exiting a car at Folderol Wine Bar for Rosalía’s birthday party. Both had black outfits on.

Chalamet touched on his relationship with Jenner in an interview with GQ.

He started by discussing the fan interest in him and his love life: “I can’t say that this stuff doesn’t matter, because my intense fandom has led me to where I am.”

But he also “bristles at the suggestion that he might not be entitled to a wholly private life,” GQ’s reporter Daniel Riley wrote. Riley then gently suggested that “if he really wanted to be left alone he might not spend time with one of the four most followed people on Instagram,” referring to Jenner.

On October 25, WSJ. Magazine published an interview with Jenner. The outlet wrote that Jenner was not ready to speak about her relationship with Chalamet, but she did give her opinion on his film Dune as a sci-fi fan. “I do love that movie,” she said.

Chalamet and Jenner kicked off the month together by both attending the WSJ. Magazine Innovator Awards on November 1 in New York City. Jenner was honored with the Brand award, while Chalamet presented the Film award to director Martin Scorsese.

The couple matched in dark ensembles and sat next to each other during the dinner portion of the event. Photographers captured one shot of them at the table:

On November 11, Chalamet hosted Saturday Night Live and Jenner’s mother, Kris Jenner, hinted at her approval of the relationship with a post on Instagram related to the big gig. In what seems like her first acknowledgment of the relationship, Kris reposted the promotional video for Chalamet’s appearance on her Instagram Story. She wrote, “Tune in to SNL tonight!”

After the successful show, Jenner was seen going to the after-party in a black ensemble to show her own support for Chalamet.

At the end of the month, Jenner secretly traveled to London to support Chalamet at the premiere of Wonka. She attended the after-party, Entertainment Tonight reported, with an eyewitness saying Jenner was seen at The Corinthia Hotel, “just steps away from” Chalamet.

A source told People on December 4 that Jenner is officially calling Chalamet her boyfriend. She is “incredibly happy,” the source said, adding they had put a label on their relationship. “He is very supportive of her career and she of his. They both try to attend important events for each other.”

“He is very good for Kylie,” that source added. “Since dating him, she seems very content, relaxed and focused. Her family loves him.”

Chalamet, meanwhile, is “in awe of everything she is accomplishing [and] especially thinks she is an amazing mom.”

On December 18, during an interview with MTV’s Josh Horowitz, Chalamet made a rare comment about his appearances with Jenner after the viral clip of them kissing at a Beyoncé concert was mentioned. Horowitz had asked Chalamet what his favorite concert of the year had been, and the Wonka actor drew a blank.

“You went to Beyoncé. That is documented, I will say that,” Horowitz joked.

He laughed, “That’s right. That was great. Hard to be present.”

He then commented more on the concert, saying, “I was actually surprised. I’m not, like, Beyhive-level, but I thought I knew way more [songs]. But I guess I know some of the more basic hits.”

On Friday, January 5, Chalamet was seen driving Jenner’s Range Rover in Los Angeles, stopping on Sunset Boulevard at the Supreme clothing store. The actor was wearing a brown sweatshirt set from Pakistani streetwear label Rastah and matching shoes. His other accessories included a black baseball cap and gold neck chain.

Jenner and Chalamet attended the Golden Globes together. While the couple opted not to walk the red carpet together, they sat side-by-side during the ceremony. They were filmed kissing at one point. Fans speculated that Jenner told Chalamet she loved him in the footage based off her lip movements.

The couple was also photographed being affectionate during the broadcast:

Sources spoke to Entertainment Tonight and People about how serious Jenner and Chalamet are. A source told People: “They’re both real with each other, and things have been easy and fun. Timothée reminds Kylie to live in a very ‘present’ way, and she really likes that about him. They both push each other to be better people, and that’s a constant thing in their relationship.”

The source said of their current dynamic: “[They] are super serious and very involved with each other’s day-to-day lives, family on both sides included. On Kylie’s side, Kris [Jenner] and Kim [Kardashian] are especially supportive and think there’s so much potential.” On Chalamet’s side, “his family also sees how happy she makes him. They’re definitely beyond the ‘just having fun’ point of the relationship. Everyone on both sides sees definite potential for something real here.”

Entertainment Tonight’s source discussed their commitment to supporting the other’s career. “Things have been going very well between Kylie and Timothée,” that source said. “They are extremely supportive of one another and like to be there for each other.”

“Kylie is extremely busy and has so many of her own things going on, but she makes an effort to show up for Timothée,” they continued. “It means a lot to him to have her support and that she goes out of her way for him and the things he’s passionate about. He is so incredibly appreciative and sees a side of Kylie that she doesn’t necessarily show everyone.”

That evening, Chalamet shut down rumors sparked at the Golden Globes that he and Jenner had drama with Selena Gomez. Fans speculated that Gomez had told Taylor Swift that Jenner blocked her from taking a photo with Chalamet.

Chalamet spoke to a TMZ reporter who followed him and asked repeatedly about the drama. Chalamet said that “yeah, of course” he and Gomez were cool. When asked if Jenner and Gomez had any “beef,” he said “no,” adding that the three stars, “we’re all good.”

Jenner briefly addressed fan theories that dating Chalamet changed her style in an interview with The New York Times. “I don’t know how I feel about that,” she responded. “I just don’t want to talk about personal things.” She avoided discussing him otherwise.

On May 29, a source told Entertainment Tonight that Chalamet and Jenner are still dating even though they hadn’t been seen together recently. “Kylie and Timothée are still seeing each other and happy,” the insider shared. “They don’t need to try to make things work and it just comes naturally to them. Their relationship is easy. They make an effort to see each other when they can and stay in touch when they’re not geographically close to one another. They're in constant and fluid communication. They see a long-lasting relationship together.”

One source told People that Jenner and Chalamet were spotted on a double date at New York City’s Tatiana by Kwame Onwuachi on Thursday, May 23. A second source told the outlet that Jenner and Chalamet “are very low-key when it comes to their relationship and like to keep it that way.”

On June 28, Jenner and Chalamet were photographed at TCL Chinese Theatre, having a movie night. Both wore black masks as they walked alongside each other. Chalamet was in an all-black outfit, while Jenner wore a white strapless top with black pants. It marked their first sighting in months. See the photo here.

Sources spoke to People and Entertainment Tonight about Jenner and Chalamet’s relationship.

People’s source said on July 2, “Things are great with Timothée. Kylie is happy. They are both busy, but making time to see each other, especially on the weekends. He’s been working in NYC. She’s visited him, and he’s also been back to L.A. some weekends. They’re making it work.”

“They like to have alone time and spend time with Kylie’s family and each other’s friends,” they continued. “They cook at home, go to dinners, travel when they can, play board games, and are just their authentic selves together. They are both honest with each other and there isn't any void of communication.”

The source finished by stressing how much Chalamet adores Jenner: “He loves her so much and is respectful to her entire circle. Things are blossoming between them more and more every day.”

Photos of Chalamet and Jenner leaving the same private jet were published hours before her interview came out on August 13. Chalamet had joined Jenner on her 27th birthday cruise. The Kardashians star enjoyed a trip to the Bahamas with Chalamet and a “small group of close friends,” according to a source speaking with People.

“It was a nice break for her. She’s incredibly happy with him. She’s never been in love like this before,” the insider continued. “He’s great for her...Her family loves him. He’s so discreet and always has her back. He’s very much a gentleman and everything that Kylie deserves.”

The source added, “They are very serious.”

She later shared a carousel of photos from her trip, captioning it, “Best birthday ever??”

While Chalamet and Jenner continued to keep their relationship private, Jenner was caught on film having a sweet moment with Chalamet’s older sister, Pauline, who attended the Coperni show that Jenner walked in on October 1. The women were filmed talking and exchanging a hug after the show in Disneyland Paris.

On October 12, Chalamet and Jenner were seen reuniting on a rare outing in New York City. They enjoyed pizza at Little Charli in the West Village in an image shared on social media. There was also a brief clip posted of them shared by X. Jenner was wearing a white T-shirt and black pants and Chalamet was in a blue hoodie.

In Jenner’s November 2024 ELLE cover story, released on October 23, Jenner spoke about why she won’t discuss her love life. “I think it’s important to keep things to yourself,” she said. “It’s hard for me to make a decision by myself sometimes, so the opinion of the whole world…it can be tough.”

On December 10, Chalamet and Jenner had a rare but sneaky date night. Jenner attended the after-party for A Complete Unknown’s Los Angeles premiere, E! reported. Eyewitnesses told the outlet that Chalamet was seen holding Jenner’s hand and that they stayed together “the whole night.” The outlet wrote that he also introduced her to his co-stars.

#6657. 8 Pantry Items Pro Organizers Say You Should Toss ASAP

Your expired spices and stale snacks are taking up prime shelf space.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.

Dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value. Getting rid of them will actually help you identify the pantry items that you can still use before they go bad. But how can you keep your pantry organized more regularly, and what exactly should you throw away?

Go through every item in your pantry at least twice a year, recommends Nicole Gabai, professional organizer, founder of B. Organized, and author of The Art of Organizing: An Artful Guide to an Organized Life.

If a twice-yearly check-in feels too daunting, consider a weekly five-minute check-in to discard expired goods, says Shaniece Jones, professional organizer and founder of Closet Therapy. “Organize by accessibility and intention,” she says. “Keep your daily go-tos at eye level, heavy items like large cans of oil and bottled water on lower shelves, and seasonal or rarely used items up high.” Labels, Lazy Susans, and drawer dividers are some of her go-to tools for organizing the pantry.

As you start cleaning, check off the following items—these are some of the most common pantry items our organizing experts find past their prime.

While many shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, are still safe to eat past their expiration date, you should still check for signs of spoilage. “You can tell canned goods have spoiled if they are rusted, or if you see the cans bulge or dent,” Gabai says.

Labeling pantry items helps you check how long they’ve been open. For opened packages and bulk goods you’ve decanted into containers, write the date on the label so you know when you opened them.

Spices that have lost their smell? Time to go. “If it smells flat or just not aromatic, then it needs to be replaced since it will add very little, if any, flavor to what you’re cooking,” Gabai says. She also notes that ground spices typically last one to two years, while dried herbs can last up to three years.

“Baking ingredients like flour, baking powder, and baking soda can lose their effectiveness over time,” says Meaghan Kessman, founder of Meaghan Kessman Home Organization.

Eventually, flour will go bad, but how long it takes to get rancid depends on how it’s stored and the type of flour. In general, Gabai says it will last at room temperature for six to eight months. She recommends storing it in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer.

“Check for expiration dates and any signs of spoilage, such as clumping or an off smell,” Kessman says. “If you’re unsure, test baking powder by adding a teaspoon to hot water—if it bubbles, it’s still good to use.”

We often buy cooking oils in bulk, but keep in mind that they eventually go bad. “Oils and fats, such as olive oil, vegetable oil, and shortening, can become rancid if stored for too long. Rancid oils have a sour or off smell,” Kessman says. “Always check the expiration date and store oils in a cool, dark place to keep them fresh longer.”

Gabai recommends storing oils in a cool, dark place and disposing of them properly; freeze in a zip-top bag, then toss in the trash (never pour down the drain).

These pantry staples are oil-rich, so they spoil faster than you might think. “They can last about 6 months at room temperature, but if you freeze them, they can last a year or more,” Gabai says.

“Snacks and cereals can go stale quickly once opened,” Kessman says. She recommends checking expiration dates and signs of staleness, like an unusual smell or texture.

According to Gabai, grains, rice, and beans can last about one to two years, but brown rice and other whole grains will not last as long because of their higher oil content.

“Condiments like ketchup, mustard, and salad dressings often get pushed to the back of the pantry and forgotten,” Kessman says. “Check for expiration dates and any signs of separation, discoloration, or off smells.”

Honey is the rare exception that probably isn't spoiled. The National Honey Board states that honey has a shelf life of approximately two years, although it can last much longer if stored correctly in a sealed container.

“Honey was found in the tombs of kings and royalty as far back as 3,000 years in Egypt—and it was still edible!” Gabai notes.

If you notice crystallization, Gabai recommends gently heating the honey container in a pot of water.

#6656. The 12 Best-Dressed Stars at the GQ Men of the Year 2026 Party

The GQ Men of the Year 2026 party is a wrap, and what a time it was. Where else but on menswear’s biggest night could you see Stavvy rocking a chartreuse suit, get some potential dirt about the next James Bond straight from the source, and witness Matt Damon learning that “body count” has two meanings? Now that’s Hollywood, baby!

As per usual, the evening really started cooking on the step-and-repeat, where the celebs took the “modern red carpet” dress code to heart. We’re talking swaggy suiting, fantastic gowns, and yes, even a very good pair of khakis. Scroll on to see our favorite looks of the night.

Now this is how you wear a suit. The Emmy-winning star of The Bear rolled up in an impeccably tailored pinstriped look by London-based designer Conner Ives, which was punctuated by a bright green shirt, a forehead curl, and a deep burgundy tie that matched the MOTY backdrop. As GQ’s former fashion critic Rachel Tashjian put it on Instagram: “She always looks cool, but this is the coolest she’s ever looked.”

For Garfield, no look is complete without his flowing mane of hair. It doesn’t hurt to have a crisply tailored Edward Sexton suit and an all-time classic watch from Breguet on his wrist.

Andrew Garfield in Edward Sexton. Watch by Breguet.

In Mowalowa sparkles and a Donna Summer-esque ’do, Tinashe looked every bit like the Popstar she is.

The Tony star sexed up the classic shawl lapel-jacket with a high-voltage shade of green. This is what the GQ Men of the Year party is all about: pulling off a fashion risk with A-lister-level confidence.

Stavros Halkias in Alan David, Cego, and Bottega Veneta.

Louisa Jacobson in Alexander McQueen. Jewelry by Azlee.

Belmont Cameli in Vivienne Westwood. Watch by Audemars Piguet.

A fringed glove? A pom-pom heel? A knockout of an outfit, all courtesy of Sarah Burton’s Givenchy.

What’s better than one head full of wicked micro-whisps? Two heads full of wicked micro-whisps, as seen on GQ Breakouts Shanny Wise and Jackson Walker Lewis, of the NYC DJ duo Fcukers. They each wore all-black designer duds, punctuating their looks with cut-outs and patches of leather.

Shanny Wise in Jordan Lea Allen and Haider Ackermann. Jackson Walker Lewis in Dior and Balenciaga.

#6654. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, with special thanks to the 1 Hotel West Hollywood.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. #6653. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6651. Nara Smith’s Mom’s Pasta

In our Cooking With Friends series, friends of Delish visit the Test Kitchen to share their favorite recipes with you. Happy cooking!

This is my mom’s recipe, and it taught me what simple abundance really looks like. She’d grate tomatoes and spoon the sauce over her native South African pap (a dish made from cornmeal, similar to grits or polenta), rice, ground beef, or almost anything that needed a little love. I couldn’t believe something so good could come from a handful of ingredients, and she showed me that with this dish it’s not about adding more, but how you handle what you have.

The magic is in the grating. It separates the sweet tomato pulp and leaves the skins behind, giving you the pure heart of the fruit. Please don’t skip the beef bouillon—it gives the sauce its deeper savory backbone. I love this tossed with freshly made spaghetti or tagliatelle, though dried pasta works beautifully, too—exactly like my mom makes it. You can enjoy this year-round, but it’s especially delightful in summer, when tomatoes taste like the sun.

#6650. Was This the Biggest Week in Sneakers of 2026?

As we inch towards the end of the year, there’s always a massive holiday rush in the sneaker industry (in addition to, well, everywhere else). Annual seasonal drops like the reliable Black Friday and Holiday XI launches from Jordan Brand, plus every major label trying to end the year on the highest note possible, make November and December some of the most exciting times to be a sneakerhead. To be fair, 2026 certainly still has some gas in the tank—plenty of us are already looking ahead to the return of the “Space Jam” Air Jordan 11 next month. Still, this week stands out even in an already crowded release calendar—in fact, I’m inclined to say it’s the biggest and best week of sneaker releases this year has had to offer so far.

Nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year. Reebok’s gradual revitalization takes a massive step in a fun, innovative new direction. And over at Converse, one of the most reliable celebrity designers in the footwear world is dropping some of his best work yet. Start drafting an apology letter to your credit card for everything you’re about to do with it—these are just a few highlights from the biggest, boldest week of sneakers in 2026 yet.

Who said anything about Samba fatigue? Turns out all it takes to make one of the most gen-pop shoes of the last decade feel brand new is a take like the one offered this week by Adidas Consortium collaborator Invincible, a Taiwanese brand that’s quickly establishing itself as a can’t-miss partner for the Three Stripes. Alongside a stellar line of apparel the brand has savvily outmaneuvered any semblance of cultural exhaustion with one of Adidas’s signature silhouettes by keeping it simple: They’ve outfitted the silhouette in a premium black unstructured leather and, bafflingly, a dress shoe sole rather than the Samba’s traditional gum rubber. With perforated Stripes and detailing that mimics those found on dressy leather brogues, it’s an instant contender for sneaker of the year…even if it just barely qualifies as one. This one goes on sale on November13, but with a catch—it’s an Asia exclusive. Pray to the resale market gods.

Nike has been struggling to find their next big-name collaborator, but in the meantime, some old favorites are still holding strong. One of those names is Union, the Los Angeles-based boutique founded by streetwear giant Chris Gibbs. This week, the brand is offering a buzzy iteration on the classic Nike Dunk that comes in a luxe brown suede and a heel-less mule silhouette. Like the Invincible Samba, the MO here is that all it takes to make an old shoe feel new again is a left-of-center take. These are dropping via SNKRS and Union on November 13, for $130 a pop.

Through Reebok’s ups and downs over the last decade, there has been one shining constant: Allen Iverson, the greatest athlete they’ve ever had on their roster. AI’s shoes are always in style, so if the brand simply brought back the original Question Mid silhouette for the shoe’s 30th anniversary, it’d be noteworthy enough. This year, though, they’ve taken the shoe to a new and fairly innovative space, refitting it with modern performance enhancements, making it court-worthy for the first time in decades. Sure, you can still wear them with oversized tees and baggy shorts. But for the first time in ages, the Question could also make it back onto an NBA court (or at least the pavement at your local park). It’s priced at $170 and is available now via Reebok and select retailers.

Ever since he first inked a deal with Converse in 2017, Tyler, the Creator has been one of the best celebrity collaborators in the sneaker biz. This has only become more true since the launch of the 1908 Project last year. The endeavor has seen the pair diving deep into Converse’s archive to revive everything from classic nautical boating shoes, to a jogging silhouette that hadn’t seen the light of day in decades. Ahead of Tyler’s annual Camp Flog Gnaw festival last year, he and Converse launched their best work at the time: the Bronco Boot, a canvas and rubber-toed banger of a sneaker-boot. This year, they’re running it back on a low-top Bronco Boot silhouette—once again ahead of the festival, where we’ll likely see Tyler wearing them. Think of it as the Doc Martens 1461 to the original Bronco Boot’s Doc Martens 1460. Coming your way in four earthy colorways, these are on sale now via Converse.

Speaking of Converse and boots: One of the biggest sneaker stories of the year has been Rick Owens’s return to Adidas after a fruitful stint over at Converse. The designer’s much-anticipated return collection launched this week, with these stunners at the center of the capsule. Debuting on the runway at Paris Fashion Week this past summer, Owens’s Springblade boots are a showstopper of a return. The shoe’s upper is made from a loose textile that fits up over the ankle and a leather toe cap, but the real heat comes in the return of the Springblade sole Owens and Adidas first debuted over ten years ago. They retail for a crazy $850, and can be purchased via the Adidas Confirmed app. Rick’s gonna Rick!

#6649. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6645. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6644. Cranberry Cream Cheese Spread

Of all the incredible dips we’ve created over the years, our cranberry whipped feta dip is an internet and personal favorite—so much so that I just had to come back with an equally luxurious variation: this cranberry-topped whipped cream cheese spread. With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#6642. How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some issues we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process showed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

#6641. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6640. Mashed Potatoes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

What People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry

"Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123

Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for a max of 3 to 4 days. With all of our recipes to transform your creamy leftover mashed potatoes—like fried mashed potato balls, potato rolls, waffles... we doubt they'll even last that long.
