#6639. The Greatest Grand Theft Auto Missions, Definitively Ranked

Grand Theft Auto VI drops on November 19th, and there are many ways to prepare. I’ve been replaying every game going back to the original, with a particular soft spot for the 3D era: III, Vice City, and Rockstar's greatest achievement, San Andreas—yes, yes, I'm coming in hot. After some 13 years of GTA Online, with its perpetual content stream and microtransactions, it’s easy to forget how it all began. The franchise has consistently brought freewheeling chaos and mayhem, sure. But it has also always delivered memorable story missions, which evolved from basic lures and assassinations into something like GTA V's “Friend Request or “Reuniting the Family,” culturally scathing mini-movies which have to be played to be believed. “My least favorite mission involves Michael using a tattoo gun on me,” former Rockstar director, writer, and producer Lazlow Jones told me of the latter mission. “I still give Dan [Houser] shit about that one to this day.”

What follows is a ranking of the greatest missions in the series’ history, with one caveat: I only allowed myself four missions per game, maximum. To help sort through the clear classics and happy accidents, I talked to some of the people who made these games come alive, including Jones, former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, and West Coast rapper Young Maylay, the beloved voice of Carl Johnson. Shockingly, Maylay says he’s still fond of the infamous “Wrong Side of the Tracks.” “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” Maylay said, imitating his exasperated sensei Big Smoke. I’m not including that mission on here, though, partly because I’d like to make it out of this piece alive.

Bum. Budupup-budum. For a lot of us, that theme was the beginning of our Grand Theft Auto journey. What follows is barely prologue. There's an ambush on the Callahan Bridge, an escape with 8-Ball, and a drive to a safe house in Portland, Liberty City's Brooklyn-by-way-of-Queens industrial borough. You do not fire a single shot. And yet each playthrough already looked different. Did you open the short manual and splay the map across your bedroom floor, or drive blind to the edge of the Red Light District?

"The most memorable mission for me was the first one I ever played, 'Give Me Liberty,'" Lazlow told GQ. Once the host of Technofile, a syndicated show about technology and video games, Lazlow showed up at Rockstar’s Manhattan offices in 2001 to report a radio piece. Not long after, he was spoofing American radio himself as the iconic voice of Chatterbox FM.

"[Former Rockstar CEO] Terry Donovan brought over a copy of the game the day it came out. Dan [Houser] had given me a PlayStation 2,” Lazlow continued. “I'd worked on the radio for the game all summer with Dan but I hadn't actually seen it. After the cinematic ended, I got into the car and Head Radio came on and I'm driving through town. It blew my mind."

Crazy what a difference three years can make. The Donald Love of GTA III is a composed real-estate scion with a media empire. Liberty City Stories, set in 1998, shows you the man before the polish, who’s way more overt about his hunger for power — and human flesh.

The mayoral race is his project, and Toni Cipriani is his instrument. Toni guns down the incumbent mayor R.C. Hole, somehow engendering only one star. "Steering the Vote" then puts him behind the wheel of a campaign van, zooming across Staunton while the loudspeaker blares: “O'Donovan is a communist!” “O’Donovan hates America!” or “A vote for Love is a vote for happiness!” The van has to reach specific stops before the messaging triggers, which means the game is literally grading you on how much of the world you can seduce. GTA may have predicted everything from Ozempic culture to billionaire doomsday prep, but there was no forecast sharper than this one.

For most of Rockstar’s history, the studio—technically a U.S. company, but with a British development team—has made its bread and butter satirizing America, and nothing has been off the table. But in London 1969, the first of two expansion packs for the original Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar transplants its crime sandbox to London in the late ‘60s, where the Brits take center stage. (“Who gave Paul McCartney a shotgun?” one YouTube commenter asks.) Broken up into chapters, the seminal “Dead Certainty” draws on the high-flying exploits of the real-life Kray twins, the foremost perpetrators of organized crime in London’s East End at the time, who rubbed elbows with politicians and entertainers before ultimately being locked away for life.

Grand Theft Auto is a game about many things, but one of the first things it was—and still is—is a game about cars. If San Fierro’s underrated main story missions aren’t enough (yes, I know, Cesar. The yay is leaving San Fierro again), head on over to Easter Basin for the best edition of “Exports and Imports.” The concept dates back to the original GTA, where it was called “Crane Bonuses,” but it’s a classic here because of its sheer scale. What starts at the docks turns into a mad hunt across the entire map of San Andreas, finding and then delivering 30 specific vehicles.

San Andreas has 212 defined vehicles, more than twice as many as Vice City. You start learning the taxonomy—how to tell a Remington from a Sabre and an Infernus from a Cheetah—and figuring out where certain vehicles turn up. The Camper can be found on top of Mount Chiliad, meaning the hard part isn’t finding it so much as getting the lumbering thing back down in one piece. When I was younger, I never really appreciated these side missions. Now, I love how they slow the game down and make you observe all the GTA sandbox goodness you might otherwise race past.

Rockstar has a long, cruel history of giving you a remote control and trolling. But unlike “Supply Lines” or “Demolition Man,” there’s a certain genius to this one. Vic Vance pulls up outside the Mendez compound and, instead of going in like a cowboy, climbs into a van to command a newfangled robot servant, Domestobot. At this point the game becomes a butlering simulator: Fetch a drink, light a cigar, and clean the floor, all the while trying to crack a drug kingpin’s basement safe. Rockstar didn’t forget about our charming robot after this, either. In GTA V, Radio Los Santos host Big Boy laments the Domestobot future that never arrived: "We have internet glasses, but not our own robot butler!”

In 1995, at age 17, Blair Renaud joined what became Rockstar Canada (now Rockstar Toronto), and stuck around long past his original contract, eventually becoming a technical director. “I basically walked into the boss's office and was like, ‘I'm not leaving. I'll do whatever you want,'” Renaud told me. After designing the London ‘69 map without ever having set foot in England (“I just winged it”), he and his entire Toronto office were put on QA duty for Grand Theft Auto 2, with its grim retro-futurist Anywhere City and sharper graphics.

GTA has always played with consumption (Donald Love likely ate his real estate mentor, Avery Carrington) but “Hot Dog Homicide!” is GTA2 at its most dastardly. In the original PC/Dreamcast version, you steal a bus, load it with civilian passengers, and deliver them to a Russian mob boss's meat grinder to satiate his army. “I think [GTA] was actually more controversial [in the beginning] about the crime, rather than just the violence,” Renaud said. “It was like ‘Oh, I'm like stealing people's cars and running them over.' It was a little bit more real.” For all the creative choices the series has been pilloried for in the ensuing years, a mission like “Hot Dog Homicide!” wasn't nearly as explosive then as it would be today.

I always get excited about missions that let you revisit a location you've already seen, especially when the game gives you a reason to see it differently. “Bury the Hatchet” sends Michael and Trevor back to North Yankton, the snowy Midwestern state where GTA V began, where the two men start digging into the events of the botched bank heist that set their lives on their current course.

It’s San Andreas’s “St. Mark’s Bistro” done better. Instead of briefly dropping you into a familiar location for a quick hit of nostalgia, GTA V actually lets you spend some time knee-deep in the snow. Michael and Trevor each retrace the events of the heist; Trevor unearths a coffin marked with Michael’s name, only to find Brad’s decomposing body inside. Ultimately, the two men aim guns at each other. Michael has spent much of the game on his high horse insisting that he’s changed, while Trevor, always the firecracker, is at least honest about exactly who he is.

Another great LCS mission that adds to Liberty City lore. Donald Love sends Toni to explosives expert 8-Ball (who still has functioning hands at this point) to raze an entire neighborhood, Fort Staunton, and pave the way for his Panlantic deal. With the Forellis giving chase, Toni has to get a van loaded with explosives to the site, then race through tunnels planting charges beneath the neighborhood. No way those tunnels aren’t at least a little inspired by Die Hard with a Vengeance. After the biggest explosion in GTA history (not bad for a PSP game), the National Guard can be found roaming the neighborhood. And by GTA III, Fort Staunton is teeming with scaffolding, construction pits and Cartel members, a neighborhood still reshaping itself after Toni’s seismic contribution.

There are few things more San Andreas than being handed a shoddy military plane by a mysterious government agent and being told to fly it across the state without being detected by radar. “N.O.E.” is the greatest test of your skills acquired in the Pilotwings-esque gauntlet, “Learning to Fly.” Fly too high and the military shoots you down; fly too low and the terrain dings you first. The mission captures just how far Mike Toreno has pulled CJ from the streets and into the shadowy world of government conspiracies.

Greg Johnson, a hip-hop journalist who became Rockstar's senior researcher from 2003 to 2020, traces those wild Toreno missions to the 1992 film Deep Cover. Most people know it through its title song, Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg's first record together. But the film itself touched on government corruption and drug trafficking in Southern California.

“Loved that Dan [Houser] put some Deep Cover-inspired missions in GTA SA with Mike Toreno basically playing Agent Carver and CJ as John Hull,” Johnson said. “I definitely talked to [Houser] a lot about Deep Cover, but he was also having conversations with [West Coast hip-hop producer and Rockstar writer] DJ Pooh, who personally knows [drug lord] Freeway Rick [Ross] about that era, and reading up on books and reports…as they wrote the game.”

Heavy metal band Love Fist is in a pickle. Think Speed, only with a limo, and even thicker Scottish accents than Groundskeeper Willie. The mission is straightforward, but not easy: drive the limousine across the city while keeping the momentum steady enough to hold off detonation. It’s also a testament to how Vice City could turn even its tertiary characters into stars. Love Fist barely occupies a sliver of the game, yet they've stuck around as memorable rockstars for more than two decades. Obbe Vermeij, longtime Rockstar North technical director, also has a soft spot for the mission. “Particularly funny,” he notes, “because the Love Fist voices are just guys from the office.”

There isn't a single on-rails shooting sequence in Grand Theft Auto that I've ever passed easily. Doesn't matter how many times I've played. I’m no deadeye. Luckily, in “Reuniting the Families,” there’s plenty packed in before we get to that. This is back when CJ, Sweet, Ryder and Big Smoke are all still homies, and when the vast map of San Andreas is still centered on the few-mile radius around Grove Street. You head to a motel with the intention of saving the hood, only to find it crawling with SWAT. After battling your way through the rooms and taking down a helicopter on the roof, you escape by car with the cops still in pursuit. Smoke is behind the wheel while an AK with unlimited ammo is placed in your hands. The cops can even climb onto the car and try to wrestle the gun away from you. It’s a wild, arcade-style sequence, but also one of the last hurrahs for the homies before betrayal and more nonsense from that bastard Frank Tenpenny. Fittingly, the getaway car flies straight through a Sprunk soda billboard reading “A Taste of Things to Come.”

“Cop Land” is peak bromance between Tommy and Lance, before the latter decides to ruin the movie. It’s also a snapshot of just how much more active and assertive Vice City’s main character is than man-of-no-words Claude, made all the more credible by the late Ray Liotta’s swagger in the role. Tommy isn't merely taking orders and working his way up someone else's criminal ladder. By this point, he's building the Vercetti Estate into his own empire and making his own destiny.

In “Cop Land,” the entire northern portion of the first island experiences a demographic shake up and now consists of exactly two assets: cops on foot in tan and brown and cops in green police cruisers. First, Tommy and Lance have to steal cop uniforms, a step that can get clunkier than it should when the garage door won't shut with the right number of cops inside. From there, you head to North Point Mall in disguise, plant a bomb and hightail it out of there with a five-star wanted level. Vice City’s officers were particularly bloodthirsty, and getting to a Pay 'n' Spray with Lance still intact—my man is drawn to dumb deaths—was one of my greatest teenage achievements.

Dubai-born real estate heir Yusuf Amir can buy anything. So naturally, the thing he wants most is an experimental attack helicopter parked on an arms dealer’s yacht. Rockstar was mining Gulf excess for laughs more than a decade before Dubai Bling and Love Is Blind: Habibi. Yusuf’s gaudy apartment tells you everything you need to know about him. There’s a miniature model of Algonquin laid out in his penthouse, as if the entire city were already one of his properties, and a giant dollar sign mounted on the wall. He dances to “Arab Money,” peppers his speech with hip-hop slang, and adopts the mannerisms of a culture he knows nothing about. Luis, unsurprisingly, is not particularly moved.

That makes “Sexy Time” the perfect introduction to him. Boat out from the marina, slip past the patrol and steal the Buzzard. Only, mid-flight, Yusuf calls and asks you to turn around, blow the yacht apart and run down what’s left of the arms dealers. For those who felt GTA IV took itself way too seriously, The Ballad of Gay Tony was a breath of fresh air. “Yusuf Amir is one of my all time favorite characters Dan [Houser] created,” Lazlow said. “The dialogue in this mission is hysterical, and he's constantly trying to sound street while going on about building luxury condos.”

The final chapter in the InterGlobal Studios asset arc turns Vice City into a formidable platformer. Tune in to Flash FM (Talk Talk’s “Life’s What You Make It”) or Fever 105 (Kool & The Gang’s “Summer Madness”) as Tommy leaps across rooftops on his trusted PCJ-600 bike in a single bound—though it’s far more likely that you’ll tumble to the streets at least once. There’s a delicate balance required for each stunt jump, but also a sense of reward once you master timing and speed.

This mission is, as the kids say, vibes. Something about scaling the ‘80s skyline by night while the rest of the city sleeps is unforgettable, along with the hilarious payoff, when Tommy triggers a spotlight that projects a massive X-rated image promoting adult performer Candy Suxxx (née Candice Shand) onto the side of a building. The most memorable GTA characters have a way of appearing in multiple forms: voices on the radio, bodies in cutscenes and, here, as advertising beamed across the world itself.

Small-town America gets the GTA treatment in “The Paleto Score.” Michael, Franklin and Trevor roll into sleepy Paleto Bay to rob the Blaine County Savings Bank, but the getaway quickly becomes less Ocean’s Eleven and more like Terminator or even MechCommander. Even before the heist, Lester, the master of elaborate setups, proves to be an unlikely master of conflict resolution too. His dry little “Hello, Franklin” to break up another Michael and Trevor spat still has me in stitches.

What starts as a relatively conventional bank job becomes a slow, lumbering march through an entire town, with our antiheroes mowing down cops, SWAT and eventually the military along the way. There’s even a reward for going overboard. One of the gold-medal requirements is to fire more than 4,000 bullets — because apparently, just robbing a bank wasn’t impressive enough.

Every time we see our hippie friend The Truth, his missions get better. In the apex of his mission tree, “Black Project,” CJ infiltrates Area 69, Rockstar’s twist on Area 51. There’s a stealth way of entering the maximum security facility, but that’s not nearly as fun as going in guns blazing. The level abounds with hilarious one-liners (“Get the General Mills on the line!”) and lab announcements (“Tonight’s menu is posted in the canteen. Barf bags can be ordered from Human Resources.”).

After GTA III’s and Vice City’s limited interiors, San Andreas gives you lively environments like Area 69, where you can disappear down corridors, into laboratories and through underground tunnels. And once CJ steals the coveted jet pack prototype, it becomes a way to fast travel across the state of San Andreas, bringing a whole new perspective to the final hours of the game. “The Truth. He stayed high as a motherfucker talking about conspiracy theory shit,” Young Maylay said. “But he would hit it on the head.”

Niko spends much of GTA IV doing other people’s dirty work. By “Late Checkout,” the diamond deal has gone so badly that Ray Boccino has lost his money, his diamonds and what remained of his patience. Isaac Roth, the diamond dealer who helped blow up the deal, is hiding in the Majestic Hotel. Ray wants him dead.

This mission is a choose-your-own-adventure affair. You can take the elevator and fight your way up through the guards, floor by floor, or use the window-cleaning platform outside to reach the penthouse from above and then fight your way back down. Either way, Niko eventually has to work his way through the hotel, killing Roth and his associates before making his escape.

It’s Rockstar’s take on the Plaza Hotel, minus Tim Curry, turned into a bonafide shooting gallery. Bonus points if you shove the front desk manager, who may respond by hopping over the desk to fight his own bellman.

Phil? Phil Collins? That's right. The former Genesis drummer and self-styled “Little Elvis” made gaming history by becoming the first real-life celebrity to lend his name and likeness as well as his voice to GTA. Like Vice City, VCS is inspired by the ‘80s TV drama Miami Vice; Philip Michael Thomas, who played Ricardo Tubbs on the show, voices Lance Vance in both VC and VCS, and Collins, as it happens, guest-starred on the series in 1985, as con man Phil Mayhew.

In this mission the Mob is after the Brit, and Vic has to ward them off. It all comes to a head during “In the Air Tonight” at Hyman Memorial Stadium. You're up top clearing Forelli saboteurs looming in the rafters while Phil is down below working the crowd.

For the man voicing Vic, this history wasn't lost on anyone. "Miami Vice was literally my favorite show as a little boy," said voice actor Dorian Missick. "I still have pictures of me in what I call my Miami Vice suit. One year, my mom let me get a little suit that they used to wear, but the collar’s turned up. I wore something like that for Easter. So to me, it was my opportunity to kind of be on the Miami Vice episode that I never got a chance to do. So all of these things, the Phil Collins of it all, and just that energy of it — it was exciting to be a part of that."

“Caida Libre,” Spanish for “free fall,” is one of those missions that finally makes the sprawling expanse of GTA V’s San Andreas feel like one cohesive playground. Michael and Trevor are hired by Martin Madrazo to take down a plane carrying his cousin Javier. Michael starts things off by shooting at the aircraft from Galileo Observatory with a sniper rifle.

The best part is the handoff, a seminal showcase of GTAV’s character-switch mechanic. First, Michael is coolly shooting down a plane from a mountaintop, and moments later you’re controlling Trevor, flying down country roads on a Sanchez motorcycle, chasing the falling debris like a man following his destiny. Eventually, Trevor finds Javier, kills him and climbs into the wrecked plane to retrieve the package. And, because this is Trevor, the mission ends with Trevor pining after Martin’s wife, Patricia, and kidnapping her. So much for the moral of Obsession.

When GTAIII first dropped, I spent the first few hours of the game gazing longingly across the river to Staunton Island, imagining what came next. Back in those days, Grand Theft Auto’s world opened up in stages and phases, trusting players to forgo instant gratification. That little stretch of water felt like the portal to another world entirely.

After Claude is victim of a double-cross, Maria helps him flee from Portland to Staunton where he meets his next boss, Asuka. But here’s the rub: Claude first has to prove he’s no longer the Mafia’s strongman, which means gunning down the beloved don Salvatore Leone in the heart of his turf. Once the deed is done, the Leones turn on you for the rest of the game, transforming the St. Marks neighborhood into a veritable “shotgun hell,” as YouTuber The Professional dubbed it in a video rant a few years ago. “Sayonara Salvatore” is thrilling enough. But its lasting impact on the open world is what players still can’t stop talking about.

If “Three Leaf Clover” feels familiar, that’s because it is. The mission is Rockstar’s loving homage to Michael Mann’s Heat. Niko joins Packie McReary and his brothers to rob the Bank of Liberty, complete with suits, masks, enormous bags of cash, and a getaway that quickly turns into a war through the streets of Liberty City.

There’s a little Point Break in there too: A civilian tries to play hero inside the bank, killing Michael Keane before being killed himself, echoing a similar moment in the 1991 film. Then comes the seemingly endless firefight through Algonquin’s neighborhoods, followed by an escape into the subway tunnels — the best transit system, by the way, in GTA history.

Vermeij says that in GTAIV, missions were often centered more around story than gameplay, but both are top-notch here. “These scripts could get quite big,” he said. “Thousands of lines in some cases…With every fix the script got a little more complicated.” This is GTA IV at its most cinematic, channeling the American crime movies and cop thrillers that have long shaped the series, all the while paving the way for GTAV’s slew of heists. “Four Leaf Clover,” though, remains the gold standard.

#6638. Katy Perry Shares Personal Photos of Her and Justin Trudeau From Their Baby2Baby Gala Date Night

On Saturday, Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau made a rare red carpet appearance at the Baby2Baby Gala. But Perry later shared her own photos from their night out supporting the charity. She posted several romantic shots of her and Trudeau in their matching looks on Instagram and tucked in one shot of them at the event with Zooey Deschanel and Jonathan Scott.

“Always a joy to sparkle for @Baby2Baby and celebrate the work they’ve done over the past 15 years ✨,” she wrote. “ICYMI: Every year, Baby2Baby reaches 1.5 million children in need across all 50 states, through homeless shelters, domestic violence programs, foster care, hospitals, and school districts, as well as children who have lost everything in the wake of disaster. I am so proud to be a small part of this incredible organization and to partner with them on @fireworkfoundation ♥️”

Perry previously shared photos with Trudeau to mark her 42nd birthday, revealing they went on a trip together. “Climbed to level 42 this week!” she wrote on October 29. “Was feeling indifferent about the inbetweeness of age 42…Then it was explained to me that 42 is actually the answer to everything. Though I still don’t understand, I’m ok with turning 42 as long as I can turn 42 with you ♥️ back to living…”

Perry and Trudeau have been dating for more than a year. In September, the singer called him the love of her life in an interview with People.

She looked back on her past year of healing, telling the outlet, “I learned how to step back into my purpose, and I got the greatest gift from this [Lifetimes] Tour: I got to meet the love of my life.”

Reflecting on her feelings just before meeting the former Canadian prime minister, she said, “I always wanted this epic, legendary love, and I was talking to my therapist about it: Everything in my life is epic, but this is kind of the missing puzzle piece—then it showed up.”

She also opened up about her boyfriend’s support of her music career, saying, “He knows the words, he’s supportive, and he’s in awe; it’s super healing. He is really heart-centered, and I think that we align in that way. I’m so grateful.”

#6637. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6635. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6634. Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond

After a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney. There’s a new James Bond—and his name is Robert Pattinson.

The announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a new creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in February 2025, four years after No Time to Die was released. Now, Pattinson will tux up as the seventh cinematic Bond under the stewardship of super-producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal and the vision of GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, marking arguably the biggest role of the 40-year-old London-born actor’s career.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Rumors of Pattinson’s selection caught fire in October, when delays on The Batman Part II gave him a window to audition for Bond at Berkshire’s Bray Studios, alongside peers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and an unnamed fourth actor. The chatter heightened a couple weeks later when various British tabloids suggested that Turner, O’Connor, and Lowden were each the preferred choice to satisfy the demands and responsibilities of the beloved British action hero—heightening suspicion that a final decision was looming. According to THR, the finalists were judged “based on stunts, camera presence.” But Pattinson’s last-minute arrival clearly tipped the scale.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” said Villeneuve in a statement to THR. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

It’s both a particularly inspired and obvious choice. Pattinson’s physical traits and characteristics hue close to Ian Fleming’s original Bond—tall and slim, with dark hair. He’s already a bona fide movie star, the current face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise; meanwhile, the selection catches him at the tail end of another booked-and-busy year. Unlike his auditioning peers, the acclaimed actor will enter the franchise well-experienced working in IP and with big-name directors. After co-leading this spring’s The Drama, he chewed up scenes as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (the second time working with Nolan after Tenet), made a creepy turn as Chris Hansen in Primetime, and will close 2026 as Scytale in Dune: Part 3—now the first of future Villeneuve collaborations, a relationship that surely helped him acquire his license to kill.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” Pascal and Heyman stated jointly to THR. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

The decision to hire a movie star isn’t a risky choice, but there’s not much precedent within the franchise—especially recently. When he succeeded Pierce Brosnan as Bond in 2005, beating out Clive Owen, Michael Fassbender, and Henry Cavill, Craig boasted an under-the-radar resume. He’d just come off Matthew Vaughn’s crime thriller Layer Cake, but otherwise had played supporting roles in Road to Perdition, The Mother, and Enduring Love. His only big-budget studio experience came several years earlier as Angelina Jolie’s love interest in Tomb Raider.

Naturally, the British press drew its fangs upon his selection, critiquing everything from his general obscurity to his physical features, which stood in stark contrast to previous Bond actors. “The Mane’s Blond, James Blond,” chirped The Irish Times, while The London Daily Mirror played with the same pun: “The Name’s Bland … James Bland.” At his official introduction to the press along the Thames, Craig arrived on a speedboat wearing a life vest, attracting instant mockery—the first of several digs about his less-than-sleek aesthetic and physical abilities. (One tabloid insulted an on-set sunburn and his inability to drive a stick shift car.)

Pattinson, however, has mostly conjured genuine excitement—not in spite of, but because of, his extreme familiarity with moviegoers, dating back to his Young Adult days in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises. Since then, over the last decade-plus, his eccentric characters and commanding screen presence immediately qualifies him as someone “stirring and exciting and different,” descriptors that Pascal said she prioritized in their methodical search.

Thanks to director Martin Campbell, Casino Royale returned the Bond franchise to earth and established Craig as a grounded, gritty action star in the mold of Jason Bourne. The movie ended up raking in $616 million globally, the highest earning Bond film to date, and launched Craig into four more sequels. Similarly, Pattinson will have the benefit of a highly-respected, Oscar-nominated director in his corner with experience shepherding IP into new places and eliciting compelling performances about tortured male protagonists.

With Villeneuve at the helm of this 26th installment, don’t expect another hard creative pivot; the man behind Prisoners, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune wasn’t hired to bring back the colorful, absurdist, gadget-heavy era that Austin Powers parodied throughout the 90’s. Still, new leadership means a new direction—a clean slate for Pattinson to burnish an already diverse, robust career and prove his chops again at the highest level of scrutiny.

#6633. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6632. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested just about every meal delivery service out there, and HelloFresh keeps standing out for its bold flavors. So we teamed up with the brand on a 12-week collaboration. The BA Picks collection features recipes hand-selected by our staff, and HelloFresh customers also get an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit. To choose them, we cooked many, many kits in our home kitchens and in the BA Test Kitchen, following the recipe cards exactly. We judged each one on flavor, portion size, cook time, cuisine variety, and the recipe's step-by-step clarity. This Ginger Chicken and Rice Bowl is one of those picks. Here’s what it’s like to make it at home.

As a product tester, I'm very methodical, so I was excited to help build the BA Picks collection. I got to cook a bunch of meals and decide which ones were the best—the same process I take when testing the best pizza ovens or juicers. Despite being Italian, I'm constantly drawn to Asian flavors when I cook at home on weeknights. The balance of salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic is highly addictive. It hits the spot after a long day of reviewing appliances in the Test Kitchen.

That's why the Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls caught my eye. Made with soy, Thai chili sauce, gochujang, ponzu, and Korean chili flakes, it has all the flavors I crave. It reminded me of some of my favorite BA recipes, like our Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry, a mainstay in my weeknight rotation. Can a meal kit recipe stand up to a Bon Appétit recipe that's tested over weeks of development? It was my job to find out. (Spoiler alert: It did.)

HelloFresh's Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls pair saucy ginger chicken with rice, a spicy cucumber side, and toasted peanuts on top. The recipe card rates it easy and lists a total time of 20 minutes. You can order it in two-, three-, four-, or six-serving sizes.

I have an entire container in my fridge dedicated to Asian condiments. If I were cooking this recipe from scratch, I'd have to lug the whole thing out, and the bottles would cover my counter. HelloFresh measures everything out for you, so all you have to do is open the bags and follow the step-by-step instructions.

This kit came with a "mini" cucumber that was more like a normal-size one (perfect for me, since I love cucumber salad). It also had all the seasonings, rice, toppings like peanuts, and chopped chicken breast.

The pre-chopped chicken was the underrated MVP. I rarely cook chicken at home because I hate handling it raw, plus the cleanup that comes after. (Always sanitize your cutting board and prep station after working with raw meat!) So HelloFresh came in clutch here. The only ingredients I had to pull from my own pantry were oil, salt, pepper, and a small dash of sugar.

HelloFresh instructions include photos of each step, so they're easy to follow. I started by putting a pot of rice on. Then I chopped and salted the cucumbers so they could season while I cooked the chicken. After a quick sauté in a pan, I tossed the chicken in the sauce, and it was ready. Once I drained the cucumbers, all I had to do was add the chili flakes, gochujang, sesame oil, ponzu, and sugar. From start to finish, the whole process took me all of 20 minutes. That was great, because the smells coming from each component were making my mouth water.

This dish exceeded my expectations for a meal kit. The cucumbers got a ton of umami from the fermented gochujang dressing, and the chicken was saucy, with a punch of ponzu. The ginger sauce has it all: a sweet, mild ginger flavor, a trace of salty soy, and a hint of heat. Thai chili sauce and ponzu turn it into a sticky glaze for the chicken. The cucumbers add a cooling side and a pop of color, and the peanuts on top are the finishing touch. These are flavors I'd never expect in a delivery box, and I'm super impressed.

Anyone looking to explore Asian ingredients would learn a lot from this dish. It uses gochujang, ponzu, Thai chili sauce, and Korean chili flakes. I'd never cooked with Korean chili flakes (also known as gochugaru), so I was excited to taste it. If you want a quick dinner, this recipe comes together in just 20 minutes. It's a flavorful dish without project-level effort.

The Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls hit the salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic balance I crave after a long day. The pre-chopped chicken and photo-guided steps make it easy, and there's no counter full of condiments to put away afterward. Find it in the BA Picks collection on HelloFresh, along with an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit.

#6631. Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Announcement Is Already Brewing Some Watch Drama

Throughout the years-long process of casting the new James Bond, I tried to follow the watches to an answer. When Aaron Taylor-Johnson joined the Omega family in May 2025, it felt like watching the 007 Vatican spit white smoke from its steeple. Just this past weekend, fans were still pinning red strings on their bulletin boards between Jack Lowden and the MI6 superspy when images resurfaced of the Slow Horses star wearing Omega. Since 1995’s Goldeneye, Bond has been an Omega man—a relationship later canonized in one of cinema’s most iconic line readings, when Daniel Craig confirmed his brand of choice in three stretched-out syllables: Oh-Mee-Guh.

If, like me, you were only basing your predictions on what the reported pool of potential Bonds wore on their wrists, Robert Pattinson would have been an easy name to cross off. The newly announced 007 only signed on as an ambassador for the Swiss luxury brand Jaeger-LeCoultre two short months ago! When I interviewed Pattinson about the appointment over the summer, he was effusive about his new partner: “I very rarely even wear watches, but when I tried it on, I was like, ‘That’s my favorite watch.’ I wanted to just buy it.”

Now, in addition to juggling his other iconic role as Batman, Pattinson will presumably need to balance his existing commitment to JLC with his new gig’s long-held ties to Omega. (Reps for both brands did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though JLC conspicuously posted a photo of Pattinson on Instagram a few hours after the announcement.)

During our conversation earlier this summer, Pattinson revealed what he looks for in a watch. He caught the collecting bug in March, when he wore JLC’s Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar to the Oscars afterparties. “All these other actors with their fancy watches on asked me, ‘Hey, what are you wearing?’” Pattinson recalls. “It was one of those moments where I’m like, ‘It’s kind of badass having this thing on.’”

If it’s attention-grabbing badass watches Pattinson is after, he’s in good hands with Omega. The brand is best known for supplying the watches Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin wore when they landed on the moon in 1969. Omega has been happy to create special versions of the Speedmaster for its current partners to dial up its profile. And, of course, the Swiss house continues to expand its Bond-inspired offerings: The maker recently added a “Spectre” version of the Seamaster, 007’s preferred model, to the lineup. And whenever Omega needs to drum up buzz around soon-to-be-released models, they tend to show up on former Bond Craig’s wrists during public appearances.

Speculators trying to pin down the next Bond would have had better luck if they’d read some less recent watch tea leaves. Back in 2020, Christopher Nolan released Tenet, his inscrutable but enthralling time-warp thriller in which Pattinson plays a mysterious, dapper, and charming spy involved in a high-stakes mission to save the world—about as good a preview of what the 40-year-old actor will look like as 007 as you’ll find in his filmography. And the watch on his wrist in that flick? An Omega.

#6630. Classic Stuffing

While traditional stuffing is technically supposed to be stuffed inside the turkey to cook, that isn’t actually the ideal or even recommended way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or stuffing). I've found that you’ll achieve much better results by cooking them separately. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath. It's my perfect version of the holiday side—I tested it again and again, so it was worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

What People Are Saying:"[It's] an excellent recipe you can tweak it for taste. I like to up the onion by half again and use a lot more fresh sage." - GreenClover

"Using a [mandoline] made the final preparation fast and easy. It was a big hit over a lovely meal. The dressing brought high praise from two trained chefs." - RedFish

As I mentioned above, sourdough bread is my go-to for stuffing. The first step is to bake it! You'll need 2 sheets, or do this in batches. You want to dry it out, so bake for 15 to 20 minutes.

While that's toasting, it's time to cook the aromatics. Melt some butter, then cook the onions, leeks, and garlic until your kitchen smells amazing and everything is softened.

Time for the liquids: Simply whisk eggs, broth, milk, and some fresh herbs in a large measuring cup. You can use a touch of red pepper for a hint of spice, which I highly recommend, but if you have a spice-averse crowd, you can skip it.

When the bread is done toasting, turn the oven temp up to 375°. Prepare a 13" x 9" baking dish by coating it with a thin layer of butter.

Time to combine it all together: In a large bowl, mix the bread, aromatics, and liquid ingredients and toss until combined. You can let this sit at room temperature for up to 1 hour if you're planning ahead. Dot with even more butter, then bake until crispy. You can serve this stuffing warm or at room temperature.

#6629. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6628. David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

David Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”

Duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he says of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”)

The albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, says.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”

For the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucking Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”

“Good question,” Duchovny says, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he says, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a biopic that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he says.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he said on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron said.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”

Truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons said no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I said: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”

I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”

“It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”

#6627. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#6626. The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Plan.

My friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation. I don't just bargain hunt. I bargain scour as if it were 1931.

This habit stays with me no matter if I’ve got a book on the bestseller list or if the stock market has just tanked. As a lifelong fisherman, I love angling for opportunities lolling in the currents of American commerce. I can’t stand the idea of buying a $5 gallon of milk when I know that the same milk from the same cows is lurking at a supermarket across the street for under three bucks.

With the inflationary surge of recent years, my friends have at last started to take a curiosity in the methods of my madness. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the price of sirloin steak is up 21% since January 2024. Romaine lettuce? 27%. Even a gosh darn cup of coffee will cost you over 50% more in 2026 than it did when the Kansas City Chiefs last won the Superbowl. So when Bon Appétit asked my cheapskate self if I could get through a week of groceries for below what the USDA stipulates as its “thrifty food plan,” I smiled the knowing smile of an old-timer. Bon Appétit and USDA, I accept your challenge.

The USDA established the Thrifty Food Plan in 1975 and updated it in 2021 in an attempt to model a healthy diet that hits all the food groups. The TFP, as we’ll call it here forward (to economize on words in these lean times), proposes different shopping lists for different genders and age groups. I took those 2021 numbers and adjusted them for 2026 inflation. As a man in his 50s, I was given a total allotment of $64.90 per week, and recently, I took to the weird yet familiar corners all over New York City at which I procure my groceries. Using my usual regular shopping list, I mostly beat those numbers across the board—without, as US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins recently suggested, resorting to a nutritionally suspect “$3 a meal for a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, you know, a corn tortilla and one other thing.”

However, the experiment raised a deeper question: Should I have to? But first, here’s how I did it.

Out of habit or laziness, many of us have a “favorite grocery store.” In an era of rapacious capitalism that has pushed so many Americans toward insolvency, there can be no favorites. Rather, it pays to seek out places where merciless competition drives major chains towards a common bargain basement. In Manhattan, where I live, I call these places “golden corners”—spots where Trader Joe’s, Target, and the rising star of discount grocery chains, Lidl, cluster together around a single intersection.

I’m able to easily deduce which place offers the lowest prices and run between them in a single shopping outing. While I’ll occasionally venture elsewhere for my meat and dairy (see: Chinatowns, featured later in this article), I find a good cutthroat corner serves me best when looking for animal protein.

Note: There is no beef on this list. For climate change reasons, I’ve never been a fan of the world’s most carbon-intensive protein, and to my mind, the three-dollars-cheaper-per-pound ground turkey works just fine in a Bolognese. Also note that neither the TFP nor I put any cheese on our lists either. I’m not sure why TFP refrained, but after beef, cheese is one of the most climate impactful animal proteins on the planet. The environmentalist in me also says cut the cheese.

Professional economizers often encourage us to choose vegetables and fruits with longer shelf lives that can bang around in our fridges until we’re ready to eat them. I’ve found picking the cheapest fruits and vegetables when they’re available is ultimately a better deal. For this, I turn to a staple of American urban street life: the fruit cart.

Fruit cart vendors, common in New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, buy produce wholesale and offer deep discounts, especially when shelf life is short. My go-to cart-guy in Lower Manhattan nearly always has a $1 special (cauliflower, cucumbers, asparagus, berries of all kinds) and the relationship we’ve built means he steers me toward what’s good.

What if the nearly overripe berries go off? To this I say: There is no berry too off that can’t be made into jam (which saves you in the miscellaneous category at this article’s end). As for salad greens, while the mainstream shopping world wrings its hands over cyclosporiasis, I’ve found that joining a community garden circumvents the dreaded disease while also purging the scourge of inflation from your wallet. My community garden costs me about $50 a year in membership fees, seeds, and fertilizer, plus about an hour of my time a week in tending. The buy-in amounts to roughly $0.50 per salad.

Whatever fruit carts and my garden can’t supply, I usually find at great prices in Manhattan’s Chinatown, likely because vendors have connections to a handful of small farms and wholesalers that operate outside of most mainstream supermarkets. According to the California Migration Museum, there are roughly 50 Chinatowns across America in nearly every major American city, which is to say that a lot of the country should have access to one.

Note: Even with bargain basement shopping, I only barely hit USDA’s fruit mark. This was because nearly half of USDA’s fruit budget is juice, which, to my mind, is a bit like calling ketchup a vegetable.

The TFP drives a hard bargain on grains, expecting the home shopper to plunk down $3.76 for an entire week’s worth of “refined-grain staple grains," which include rice, pasta, bread, tortillas and the like. That’s tough when a loaf of Wonder Bread at Walmart costs you $2.47. Add a single box of one-pound pasta and it could send you over-budget.

There’s a bit more give in the "whole-grain staple grains" category, which allows $6.94. But even a whole-wheat loaf from Walmart (priced at $2.97) eats up just over half of my weekly allotment.

The only way I was able to snag the bread, rice, and pasta in my weekly shop and stay under budget was by leaning on another Asian country and by working hard on my home turf.

Patel Brothers, a national chain of Indian grocery stores, sells brown and white rice as well as beans of all flavors and provenances for prices that range from $0.80 to $2 per pound. As for bread, Target’s house brand of whole wheat flour is $2.69 for a five-pound bag. About a pound and a quarter of it makes a loaf. Weekly sandwich bread therefore costs out at $0.67 per loaf.

Last and actually also least: pasta. Nobody but nobody beats Trader Joe’s buck a pound.

Shopper beware—the last-minute, forgotten miscellaneous item is often the thing that stings you most at the register. Salt, sugar, cooking oil, and coffee purchased last minute, at even a cheap store, can be double what you’d pay if you are keeping careful track of who's charging what at your local golden corner. Keeping a passive list in your head of where the best buys on miscellany live helps these kinds of rookie mistakes from happening.

Additionally, as above, a little home elbow grease can be surprisingly effective in the condiment aisle. Fruit cart fruit made into jam and an immersion-blended home mayonnaise (a commitment of two minutes max) cost you pennies. And then there’s online. I have yet to find a better deal on coffee than on Amazon.

So I did it. I filled my fridge, stocked one shelf of my pantry, and even had a little left to treat myself to breakfast after this exhausting pan-city forage. Here’s what the final numbers looked like:

Does this mean the USDA’s stingy allowance is appropriate for these ever more expensive times? That anyone can be a successful cost-cutter like me?

Um, no. My kids are grown. I’m a freelance writer with weird hours. I live in a vast, quirky city with odd corners that can cost out cheaper than parts of the developing world. A busy working mom in a food desert who can’t commit to a community garden would find the ordeal a heavy lift.

Thank you for joining me on this ride through my own personal Great Depression. But as for you, USDA, I think it’s time you upped your budget. Stop cutting things like food stamps and healthcare. Perhaps the newest iteration of Congress will be more inclined to make this happen than its predecessor. We are, after all, among the wealthiest sovereign nations in the world.

C’mon, America! Don’t be such a cheapskate.
